title: Contact-number hyperuniformity at glass close packing in infinite dimensions
summary: We investigate contact-number fluctuations of harmonic spheres near glass close packing (GCP), the amorphous jamming endpoint reached by compressing an ideal glass. Using replica theory, we show that the Gardner-unstable region shrinks toward jamming as the spatial dimension increases, allowing GCP to be approached along a stable one-step replica symmetry breaking branch in the high-dimensional limit. By coupling an external field to the local contact number, we derive the variance of the total contact number and the wave-number-dependent structure factor directly from the microscopic interactions. At GCP, the structure factor vanishes quadratically at small scaled wave numbers, demonstrating contact-number hyperuniformity. Upon weak compression above GCP, the structure factor develops a low-wave-number plateau whose height is proportional to the excess coordination. These results provide an analytical description of contact-number hyperuniformity and its breakdown upon compression.

title: Stochastic Dynamics of Domain Walls on a Racetrack: Impact of Inhomogeneity of Magnetic Anisotropy
summary: Racetrack memory is a spintronic technology that stores information in current-driven magnetic domain walls (DW), offering a promising route toward non-volatile, high-density, and high-speed memory devices. In ultrathin magnetic films, atomic-scale interface disorder can produce spatially inhomogeneous magnetic anisotropy, creating a complex spatially varying energy landscape that strongly influences DW motion. In this work, we model anisotropy inhomogeneities using a two-dimensional fractal Weierstrass--Mandelbrot function, which provides independent control over the disorder amplitude and characteristic spatial scale. Micromagnetic simulations reveal pronounced stochasticity of current-driven domain-wall transport even in the absence of thermal fluctuations. Transport is quantified by the transmission fraction, defined as the fraction of DWs that successfully reach a detector after propagating through a disordered racetrack. We investigate its dependence on current density, disorder amplitude, and the spatial scale of the anisotropy inhomogeneity. The resulting transmission statistics are described by Gaussian error-function profiles and exhibit a universal scaling behavior upon normalization by the corresponding median values. Statistical analysis of DW trajectories further characterizes the disorder-induced fluctuations of the propagation process. The variance of the random DW positions shows a pronounced dependence on disorder amplitude and is well described by the proposed phenomenological model. These results provide a quantitative framework for describing stochastic DW transport in structurally disordered racetracks and establish disorder-induced reliability limits in racetrack-memory devices.

title: Complex mobility edges from competing localization channels in non-Hermitian quasicrystals
summary: Non-Hermitian localization transitions often accompany multiple mobility edges, but their physical origin can be ambiguous. To address the issue, we introduce an extension of the Ganeshan-Pixley-Das Sarma model with both asymmetric hopping and complex onsite potential, thereby incorporating a broad range of non-Hermitian quasiperiodic chains. Its solution reveals two energy-dependent localization contributions manifested as distinct Lyapunov growth scales, whose competition determines the structure of mobility edges. We derive exact Lyapunov exponents via Avila's global theory, obtain thresholds of the two channels on complex-energy plane, and formulate a selection rule that distinguishes physical mobility edges from suppressed analytical candidates. The channel that uniquely controls localization can switch with energy, producing complex mobility edges of non-Hermitian origins. Nonreciprocal hopping further shifts the thresholds and alters the bulk energy patterns. Numerical spectra and finite-size localization diagnostics confirm the theory. Our work thus provides a unified framework for characterizing phase transitions and mobility edges under competing localization mechanisms in non-Hermitian quasicrystals.

title: Quasi-long-range order in the quantum XY model on Sierpi\'nski gaskets
summary: Fractal geometry has recently been shown to enhance the amplitude of the superconducting order parameter, but the fate of the superconducting phase on such lattices is far less clear. Classical XY models on finitely ramified fractals have no finite-temperature transition, as the energy of a vortex stays bounded as the system grows. However, that statement concerns an infinite gasket and thermal vortices, while real fractal structures are finite by construction. It also leaves open what happens at $T = 0$, where the phase competes not with temperature but with its own quantum fluctuations. In this work we address whether superconducting phase coherence survives at $T=0$. %Whether coherence survives those is the prior question, and the one we address here. To that end, we study the spin-$1/2$ XY ferromagnet, the phase sector of a Josephson network with at most one Cooper pair per island, thus capturing the maximum effect of quantum phase fluctuations, on both triangular and honeycomb Sierpi\'nski gaskets. By using vision-transformer neural quantum states optimized by variational Monte Carlo, we reach generations up to $G = 5$, that is $366$ sites for the triangular gasket and $609$ for the honeycomb one, well beyond the reach of exact diagonalization. We find that the transverse two-point correlator decays algebraically, $C_{xy}(r) \sim r^{-\eta}$ with $\eta \simeq 0.12\!-\!0.32$, independent of distance measured along the graph, along the fractal boundary, or in the embedding plane. Quantum phase fluctuations thus leave quasi-long-range order intact in the ground state. We further discuss the implication of these results for the superconducting response of a finite gasket at low but nonzero temperature.

title: Statistical Properties of the $q$-Deformed Monolayer and Bilayer Graphene
summary: We investigate the statistical properties of the $q$-deformed Dirac oscillator for monolayer and bilayer graphene in the presence of a constant external magnetic field. Using $q$-deformed creation and annihilation operators, we obtain the corresponding energy spectra and eigenfunctions, as well as their probability current densities, recovering the conventional Landau-level structures in the undeformed limit. For bilayer graphene, the lowest Landau levels are explicitly constructed within the $q$-deformed framework. The partition functions for both systems are derived using zeta-function techniques and the Euler-Maclaurin formula, allowing us to determine their main thermodynamic quantities for small values of the deformation parameter. Our results show that the $q$-deformation modifies the energy spectra, the behavior of the probability current density components, and the thermodynamic response of the systems. A comparison between monolayer and bilayer graphene reveals distinct thermal behaviors, reflecting their different Landau-level structures and highlighting the influence of the $q$-deformation on their statistical properties.

title: The Kitaev model on finite hyperbolic PBC clusters
summary: We construct and solve the three-colored Kitaev model on finite hyperbolic lattices with periodic boundary conditions. We describe a self-contained procedure which uses finite quotients of orientation- preserving triangle groups to generate regular maps on compact genus-g surfaces. From these, one can extract their lattice connectivity, plaquette structure, homology cycles and Wilson sectors while implementing consistent boundary conditions. On the example of {8, 3} and {12, 3} lattices, we enumerate a selection of quotients with up to 72 vertices, which constitute the discrete steps in a finite-size scaling analysis. For the isotropic point, corresponding to the spin-liquid phase in the thermodynamic limit, we identify the ground state superselection sectors, quantify their deviation from the homogeneous {\pi} flux sector and show how the selected flux background depends on the quotient geometry. We then discuss how the resulting ground state sector degeneracies are entirely generated by physical lattice symmetries acting on both the plaquette fluxes and non-contractible Wilson loops. Finally, we study the behaviour of the finite-size two-vison gap and matter fermion correlations. We find that the gap does not decrease monotonically with increasing system size, while one still recovers the expected algebraic decay of the correlations at the isotropic point, even for the considered modest system sizes.

title: Magnon-Phonon-Polariton Optomechanics in a van der Waals Magnet
summary: The layered anti-ferromagnet CrSBr hosts self-hybridized exciton-polaritons that couple parametrically to coherent magnons and phonons. In this work, we explore the tripartite optomechanical interaction between these quasiparticles in suspended CrSBr membranes supporting high-$Q$ breathing-type acoustic phonon modes. Using resonant pump-probe spectroscopy on the polariton state, we resolve the coupled dynamics in the $\simeq 20$ GHz range while sweeping the magnon mode across the phonon resonance with an external magnetic field. We observe an attractive magnon-phonon interaction of strength $V/2\pi = -43$ MHz, which primarily leads to phonon amplification. At the magnon-phonon resonance, we find predominantly unidirectional energy flow from magnons to phonons while the possible back-action is limited by kinetic losses of coherent magnons. Our study enables direct interfacing of collective magnetic excitations with sound and light in layered van der Waals materials, paving the way for quantum-coherent transduction in the GHz range with optical readout.

title: Optical characterization of Fermi polarons in monolayer MoSe$_2$ encapsulated in amorphous silicon nitride
summary: Amorphous silicon nitride is the leading low-loss, CMOS-compatible platform for wafer-scale integrated photonics. Encapsulating transition-metal dichalcogenide (TMD) monolayers within this platform offers a promising route towards scalable TMD-photonic circuits. Yet the effect of this amorphous dielectric on the optical response of the monolayer remains poorly understood. Here, we compare monolayer MoSe$_2$ encapsulated in amorphous silicon nitride with a hexagonal boron nitride-encapsulated reference, using differential reflectivity and photoluminescence. Whereas the reference is dominated by the neutral exciton, the nitride-encapsulated monolayer shows attractive and repulsive polaron resonances separated by ${\sim}31$~meV, with emission dominated by the attractive branch. A quantitative comparison of temperature-dependent reflectance with a microscopic finite-temperature Fermi-polaron theory shows that the nitride induces substantial electron doping in the monolayer, with an electron density of $(0.8$--$0.9)\times10^{12}$~cm$^{-2}$. Using the extracted density and trion binding energy as the only input parameters, the theory reproduces the photoluminescence spectra up to ${\sim}80$ K in excellent quantitative agreement with experiments, thus corroborating the Fermi-polaron description of the observed excitonic response.

title: Reconfigurable 2D Lateral Heterostructure Platform for Unified Detection, Emission, and Logic
summary: Heterogeneous integration of sensing, light generation, communication, and computation typically requires specialized devices, resulting in complex interconnects, fabrication overhead, parasitic losses, and energy penalties. Developing a monolithic, reconfigurable device capable of controlling carrier generation, transport, and recombination remains a longstanding challenge. Two-dimensional (2D) lateral heterostructures offer a promising approach by combining spatially distinct domains of different charge polarity with a dynamically tunable electrostatic landscape. Here, multifunctional bilayer MoSe2-WSe2 lateral heterojunctions are demonstrated, integrating photodetection, reconfigurable electroluminescence (EL), and CMOS logic operation within a unified platform. The photodetector exhibits a responsivity of 35 A W-1, a specific detectivity of 5 x 10^13 Jones, and a noise-equivalent power of 6.3 x 10^-18 W Hz^-1/2, enabled by efficient charge separation and photoconductive gain. Under electrical injection, electrostatic gating dynamically switches the radiative recombination zone among the MoSe2 domain, lateral heterointerface, and WSe2 domain, enabling spatially programmable EL, optical multiplexing, and ternary optical logic. Furthermore, the complementary transport characteristics of the two domains enable CMOS inverter operation at 0.25 kHz. These functionalities originate from a common electrostatic framework in which the gate-tunable depletion region governs carrier extraction, recombination, and transport. This work establishes 2D lateral heterostructures as multifunctional building blocks for monolithically integrated electronic and optoelectronic systems combining light sensing, generation, and information processing.

title: Intrinsic second-order nonlinear Hall effect from perturbation theory
summary: Nonlinear transport provides an efficient probe of the electronic structure and symmetry of quantum materials. As a prominent example, the intrinsic nonlinear Hall effect has attracted considerable attention in recent years because it is independent of impurity scattering and directly reflects the quantum geometry of Bloch electrons. Here we establish a simple textbook-style perturbation theory for the intrinsic nonlinear conductivity. Based on the well-defined Bloch-state velocity, our formulation perturbatively determines the field-corrected velocity and distribution function, from which the conductivity follows directly. We further compare our approach with wavepacket-based theories and discuss their consistency.

title: Landscape index and its boundary correspondence in inhomogeneous chiral systems
summary: We define a real-space topological index from the geometry of a quadratic landscape associated with the spatial dynamics, which is governed by the zero-energy eigenvalue equation of chiral systems. The landscape index remains invariant under continuous deformations preserving the uniform exponential separation between decaying and growing spatial solutions and equals the continuum winding number in the homogeneous limit. Across an inhomogeneous interface, the difference between the indices on the two sides equals the protected net chiral zero-mode count, without requiring asymptotically homogeneous bulk regions. Explicit landscape constructions yield analytical bounds on Hamiltonian parameters and their spatial gradients that determine the indices for all profiles satisfying these bounds, without specifying their detailed spatial form. Dimensional reduction extends the landscape index and its boundary correspondence to higher-dimensional systems. The resulting bounds guarantee protected radial zero modes in effective Kitaev-type systems of arbitrary transverse codimension and identify parameter and momentum regions supporting chiral edge states in periodically modulated quantum anomalous Hall systems. For the quasiperiodic interface considered, the index difference guarantees a single protected chiral branch despite persistent modulation on both sides, as confirmed by numerical calculations. Landscape geometry thus connects real-space topology to the protected net chirality of boundary states.

title: Performance limits and benchmarking of ideal 2D topological insulator field-effect transistors
summary: Topological insulator field-effect transistors (TIFETs) have emerged as a promising alternative to overcome the scaling limits of silicon-based field-effect transistors (Si-based FETs). In this study, we establish the performance limits of ideal TIFETs and present a comprehensive benchmarking of the switching energy-delay performance of TIFETs against Si-based FETs (FinFET and LGAA) and 2-D material-based FETs ($\mathrm{MoS}_2$ and InSe) under equivalent and realistic conditions. Furthermore, we analyze the key factors influencing the switching energy-delay performance of TIFETs, including contact resistance ($R_{\mathrm{C}}$), parasitic capacitance ($C_{\mathrm{par}}$), channel length ($L$), and channel width ($W$). Notably, TIFETs achieve substantially lower switching energy and delay time, outperforming both Si-based FETs and 2-D material-based FETs, where a transition from 1-stack to 3-stack yields approximately a sixfold reduction. This benchmarking study shows that TIFETs exhibit competitive switching performance and hold strong potential for future topological electronic devices.

title: Axion electrodynamics and the advection-diffusion structure of TEM modes in hollow-conductor waveguides
summary: We present a systematic investigation of transverse electromagnetic (TEM) modes in hollow-conductor waveguides filled with a dielectric medium described by axion electrodynamics. While such modes do not propagate in conventional single-conductor waveguides, the coupling of the axion field to an external magnetic field enables their propagation. We show that the resulting TEM modes are governed by an advection-diffusion-type equation for the transverse electrostatic potential, establishing a direct mathematical connection between axion electrodynamics and advection-diffusion phenomena. We illustrate this connection through explicit solutions and field profiles for cylindrical waveguides, considering uniform and rigid rotational drift fields, both individually and in combination, as well as different values of the parameter controlling the advection-to-diffusion ratio (P\'eclet number). These results establish a transport-based framework for understanding how spatial variations of the axion-electrodynamics background shape the transverse electromagnetic fields in hollow-conductor waveguides.

title: Electrical addressing of compensated magnetic order in artificial spin ice
summary: Compensated magnetic systems, such as antiferromagnets, hold immense potential for spintronic devices thanks to vanishing stray fields, robustness to perturbations, and ultrafast dynamics. Yet, electrical writing and reading of their order remains a major challenge. Here we use artificial spin ice as a mesoscale platform in which compensated order can be engineered, directly imaged, and electrically controlled. Specifically, we demonstrate combined electrical writing and reading of a compensated state in a triangular artificial spin ice. Exploiting the orientation dependence of the spin-orbit torque switching current, we independently switch three nanomagnet sublattices through a single current channel, with the planar Hall effect providing sublattice-resolved readout. This grants access to all eight magnetization states of the triangular plaquette, including its fully compensated state, yielding a nonlinear, history-dependent electrical response. Our results establish an approach to electrically programmable compensated magnetic systems and provide an important foundation for reconfigurable magnetic devices and unconventional computing.

title: Dynamics of a Single-Domain Dissipative Magnetic Gyroscope in Electric and Magnetic Fields
summary: We formulate the coupled spin--rotation dynamics of a single-domain symmetric top ferromagnetic needle (a magnetic gyroscope) in static magnetic and electric fields. The conservative Hamiltonian contains the rotational kinetic energy, the magnetocrystalline and shape anisotropy, the Zeeman energy, the electrostatic energy of the dipole induced in the conducting needle, the linear magnetoelectric coupling, and the relativistic motional (spin-orbit) coupling. Gilbert damping is introduced, and in an electric field, Debye relaxation of the induced electric dipole of the conducting needle also results in dissipation. We give the equations of motion in the laboratory and body-fixed frames, with singularity-free quaternion kinematics. For a 120-nm-long single-domain cobalt needle in a 0.5~T field we find: (i) because the anisotropy field ($\approx 1.3$~T) exceeds the applied magnetic field, the spin reverses direction several times during the initial Gilbert-damping transient, and the parity of the number of reversals determines whether the easy axis ends up parallel or antiparallel to the spin; (ii) after the transient the needle librates about the field---precession accompanied by nutation at twice the precession frequency---with a period of about 20~ns, consistent with the libration period $2\pi(I_1/\mu B)^{1/2}$, while the Zeeman and rotational kinetic energies oscillate out of phase and the total energy is conserved; (iii) a static electric field $\mathbf E$ exerts on the conducting needle a shape-dependent polarization torque that tends to align the long axis of the needle with $\mathbf E$. The torques due to the magnetoelectric interaction and motional magnetic fields ($\lesssim1~\mu$T) are negligible compared with the polarization torque. A conducting needle can therefore serve as a magnetometer only if $E\ll E_c$.

title: Photon condensation driven by scalar spin chirality
summary: Gauge invariance forbids equilibrium photon condensation for spatially uniform electric-dipole coupling, motivating alternative routes based on orbital magnetic response. We show that triangular molecular magnets coupled to a cavity support photon condensation driven by emergent scalar spin chirality. Starting from the half-filled Hubbard model in the Mott regime, we derive an effective Hamiltonian in which virtual ring exchange couples the cavity flux directly to scalar spin chirality. Mean-field theory, collective-fluctuation calculations, and finite-size exact diagonalization reveal a phase with spontaneous chirality ordering and a macroscopic cavity displacement, together with hybrid chirality-photon excitations. The condensation threshold can be tuned electrically through the molecular chirality splitting. Our results establish emergent orbital degrees of freedom in frustrated magnets as a route to equilibrium light-matter ordering beyond conventional dipolar cavity quantum electrodynamics.

title: Quantitative Theory for the Amplitude of Fluorescence Quantum Beats from Geminate Triplet-Pair Fusion
summary: We derive the amplitude of fluorescence quantum beats caused by geminate triplet-exciton fusion from the full set of parameters that characterize singlet fission and triplet exciton dynamics. We apply the theory to tetracene and rubrene single crystals. We find that the amplitude depends on the fission time in tetracene, but does not do so in rubrene, where it is determined by the dimensionality of triplet transport. Kinetic Monte Carlo simulations reproduce the experimental data in both materials, for a fission time of the order of 200 ps and isotropic triplet transport in tetracene, and for a triplet hopping time along the herringbone axis of 200-300 ps and anisotropic transport in rubrene.

title: Ultrafast imprinting of fused ferromagnetic/antiferromagnetic skyrmions
summary: Antiferromagnetic skyrmions are promising topologically protected entities for robust storage and THz transport of information. Their generation has so far relied on slow techniques or on specific magnetic structures, which limit their integration into spintronic devices. Here, we demonstrate the imprinting of antiferromagnetic skyrmions within a few picoseconds in a coupled ferromagnetic/antiferromagnetic bilayer with a thermal laser pulse. We identify a threshold energy required to initiate the fused skyrmion phase and show that this can be modulated by a magnetic field, enabling deterministic nucleation of antiferromagnetic skyrmions. Compared to conventional slow field-cooling processes to control antiferromagnets we show that laser-induced skyrmion imprinting can be orders of magnitude faster and provides an experimentally feasible route towards ultrafast creation and manipulation of antiferromagnetic skyrmions.

title: Computational Modeling of Sublattice Magnetization in CoTb/Co/CoTb Magnetic Multilayer Nanojunctions Between Cobalt Leads
summary: In this work, we study the sublattice nano-magnetic behavior of CoTb/Co/CoTb sandwiched between semi-infinite cobalt leads. To perform the analysis, we use the Ising spin-based effective field theory (EFT), which enables us to determine the relevant magnetic exchange parameters for elemental cobalt JCo-Co and terbium JTb-Tb. The exchange interaction parameters are determined by fitting the magnetization calculated using the Ising effective-field theory to the experimentally measured temperature-dependent magnetization curves. This fitting procedure yields the exchange constants for Co and Tb, along with their respective Curie temperatures. We use the magnetic exchange parameter obtained using Ising EFT-based method is then seeded on to mean field theory (MFT) to calculate the sublattice magnetizations of CoTb/Co/CoTb arranged between semi-infinite cobalt leads. The sublattice magnetizations for every atomic layer and corresponding lattice sites in the layered ferrimagnetic nanostructures are computed separately. This allows us to analyze spin-site-specific parameters, magnetic moments, magnetization, and ferrimagnetic compensation behavior for varying eutectic compositions, particularly for \(c \leq 0.5\). The results give enhanced insight into magnetic phenomena at the local level and their general relevance in the ultra-thin layered ferrimagnetic structure dynamics confined between semi-infinite cobalt electrodes. These results are needed for the understanding of magnon transport phenomena and consequent magnetic amplification effects and are crucial to the development of spintronic technologies. Most importantly, to date, no first-principles or density functional theory research exists for sublattice magnetization in such multilayered systems. The versatile approach established in this work can also be applied to other nanostructured magnetic systems

title: Temperature Flips the Sign of the Hydrogen Response in Nanogranular Palladium Networks
summary: In nanogranular palladium networks, hydrogen uptake has two opposing effects on electrical resistance. Absorbed hydrogen scatters electrons within the particles, raising their resistance, while particle expansion narrows the gaps between them and lowers the junction resistance. Such networks are widely studied as resistive hydrogen sensors, and the sign of their net response is usually treated as a fixed property of the architecture. In networks grown by atomic layer deposition on macroporous silicon, we show that changing the operating temperature can reverse this sign at a fixed hydrogen concentration. A thermodynamic model indicates that scattering contributes less as temperature rises, allowing sub-angstroem changes in gap width to dominate. Where the two effects cancel, the network absorbs hydrogen yet gives the same reading as in hydrogen-free gas, so a leak could escape detection. Between 25 and 40 degrees Celsius, this cancellation point is predicted to rise over tenfold, crossing reported leak-alarm setpoints. At 55 degrees Celsius, the measured response stays negative but passes through a minimum, so a concentration above a setpoint can mimic one below it. Annealing at 200 degrees Celsius alters the calibration and turns the room-temperature response negative at the lowest concentration tested. Quantitative sensing therefore requires a defined thermal pretreatment and an operating temperature giving distinct signals across the intended concentration range. Response polarity becomes an operating parameter rather than a fixed property. More broadly, any nanoparticle network whose particles deform on sorption may show the same temperature-dependent competition between transport within and between particles, with implications for sensors and switches beyond palladium-hydrogen.

title: Pair distribution function oscillations at electrostatically stabilized nanocrystal surfaces reflect nanocrystal lattice periodicity
summary: Nanocrystals (NCs) stabilized electrostatically by short, multivalent inorganic ligands exhibit rich interactions and phase behavior believed to hinge on the configuration of ions at the NC surface, yet these molecular details have not previously been measured. Here we use double-difference pair distribution functions (ddPDFs) of total X-ray scattering to determine the configuration of Sn$_2$S$_6^{4-}$ ligands on PbS NCs suspended in multivalent electrolyte. The measured ddPDFs exhibit a $\sim$3-$\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$ wavelength oscillation that extends $\sim$10 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$. Comparison with a PbS NC model decorated with Sn$_2$S$_6^{4-}$ ligands indicates ligands are aligned $\sim$radially, suggesting bidentate binding. Calculated partial PDFs show that the oscillatory signal is dominated by nanocrystal-Pb to ligand-Sn correlations. A simplified model that replaces the ligand with a strongly scattering Pt atom near the NC surface confirms the oscillation period in the ddPDF originates from the NC lattice constant. Nanocrystal lattice periodicity therefore merits consideration when interpreting ddPDFs of colloidal NCs.

title: Emergent Attraction and Competing Orders near the Van Hove Singularity in Rhombohedral $n$-layer Graphene
summary: Unconventional superconductivity in rhombohedral $n$-layer graphene exhibits a rich phase diagram with multiple distinct superconducting regions, whose microscopic origins remain unclear. Here, we investigate the competition between charge-density-wave (CDW) and pair-density-wave (PDW) instabilities near the inner van Hove singularities (VHSs), using a patch renormalization-group approach with the realistic band structures incorporated. We identify two key findings. First, we find an effective attractive interaction emerging from purely repulsive interactions through RG flow in the presence of $C_3$ symmetry breaking. The resulting interaction structure, with two repulsive couplings and one attractive coupling, gives rise to competing CDW and PDW instabilities. Second, the competition is controlled by the detuning from the VHS. While CDW dominates near the VHS filling and at higher temperatures, PDW becomes the leading instability on either side of the VHS and at lower temperatures. This mechanism naturally produces two superconducting regions separated by a CDW-dominated regime, providing a possible qualitative explanation for the experimentally observed separation between SC1 and SC2.

title: Dynamics and transport in LiF using classical and machine learned interatomic potentials
summary: We perform molecular dynamics simulations of molten Lithium Fluoride, comparing the classical Buckingham and Born-Huggins-Mayer potentials with machine-learnt interatomic potentials - the MACE-MP-0b3 (small) foundation model potential, and a fine-tuned version thereof. We find that the MACE-MP-0b3, out-of-the-box, is able to accurately reproduce the experimental shear viscosity across the liquid state comparable with polarisable potentials despite not itself being polarisable. Previous viscosities computed using classical potentials are under-predicted, which has previously been attributed to a suppressed melting temperature. Prompted by this we compare the melting points of these potentials. We find that the machine-learnt potentials address the significant underestimation of the melting point of the classical potentials, though the refined potential and the foundation model differ significantly between themselves. We probe the microscopic structure and dynamics of each model to further elucidate the considerable change in viscosity between classical and machine-learnt potentials. We find that, despite their lower melting temperature, classical potentials produce considerably stiffer, higher frequency, single-particle and collective charge-transport dynamics on account of their fixed charges. However, in the long-wavelength limit, the many-body machine-learnt potentials feature more elastic collective motion that governs the diffusion of momentum and is therefore responsible for the enhanced shear viscosity.

title: quantEM: Quantitative Electron Microscopy Analysis from Differentiable Physics to Neural Priors
summary: Quantitative electron microscopy includes imaging, diffraction, spectroscopy, and tomography measurements, and the analysis of these measurements increasingly requires solving inverse problems with physical forward models. Open-source software has made many of these analyses widely available, but most packages are organized around a single modality, so that multimodal analyses require moving data between packages, and new methods cannot easily reuse the physical models and optimizers of existing ones. Here we present quantEM, an open-source Python package for quantitative electron microscopy that uses PyTorch tensors for computation and automatic differentiation, and Zarr for storage. We implement each analysis method by writing a differentiable forward model and choosing a representation, loss function, constraints, and optimizer from a library of components, so that every method runs on CPUs and GPUs, can be saved and resumed, and uses the same calibrated data structures and visualization tools. We describe the current modules, including orientation and strain mapping, direct and iterative ptychography, tomography with neural representations, and X-ray and electron energy-loss spectroscopy, and show how we assemble combined methods such as ptychographic tomography from existing components. quantEM is available under the MIT license, together with documentation, tutorials, and curated example datasets.

title: Weight-Space Programming for Materials Science
summary: A materials discovery campaign often begins with almost no measurements of the property it is searching for, and the models that rank candidates or screen the output of a generator then have to be built from those first few labels. Following recent work on weight-space programming, in which a language model writes the weights of a small network directly as text, we show that a general-purpose model, given the task in words, the names of the inputs and a network of 16 hidden units with every weight set to zero, can provide this starting point by filling in all of the weights from what it has learned about materials. With no labels, the networks of the strongest model rank experimental alloys at Spearman co-efficient = 0.64 to 0.79, where the best of five simple descriptors reaches 0.47 to 0.62. They rank the bulk modulus of crystals added during generative discovery loops at 0.95, where the inverse volume per atom reaches 0.89, and 35 phase-equilibrium targets computed with Thermo-Calc at a mean of 0.67, close to the 0.70 of an extrapolation from calculated binary and ternary data. As the prior mean of a Gaussian process they raise the ranking at five labels from 0.35 to 0.69 on alloys and from 0.15 to 0.95 on crystals, and they lower the regret of Bayesian optimization significantly on 4 of 5 experimental tasks and on 13 to 16 of 33 computed targets, depending on how multiple tests are corrected, without raising it significantly on any. The same networks also serve as the mean of a Bayesian neural network and as a screen for the samples of two crystal generators, where they do as well as standard models trained on 400 labeled structures. The gain is confined to the first tens of labels and to targets that no rule or sub-system extrapolation already ranks.

title: Frame Based Inelasticity for Strength and Fracture in Anisotropic Media
summary: A field theory is presented for predicting damage and fracture in brittle materials. Four concepts are used: a new nonlocal deformation gradient for dynamic stress analysis in anisotropic media, a new type of phase field coming from a constitutive law, the evolution of material displacement from Newton's second law, and a new incorporation of scaled strength surfaces into constitutive laws for predicting dynamic and quasi-static fracture patterns. The elastic softening is governed by the strain dynamics through the constitutive law and in this way we provide the two way coupling between strain and fracture. Simulations validating the approach for both dynamic and quasi-static fracture analysis are compared to experimental results and other simulation methods. The model is capable of predicting material strength in titania and the competition between strength and energy in soda lime glass and titana and captures dynamic crack branching in soda lime glass and concrete.

title: Electrostatic screening and nitrogen-vacancy charge states in boron-doped/nitrogen-doped diamond junctions
summary: Boron-doped diamond (BDD) enables the integration of electrical functionality with nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers, but the influence of junction electrostatics on NV charge-state stability remains unclear. In this study, we investigate the equilibrium electrostatics of BDD/nitrogen-doped diamond junctions using self-consistent Poisson-Fermi calculations. The results reveal two distinct electrostatic length scales in the nitrogen-doped substrate: a near-interface region of ionized donors that produces dominant band bending and determines the NV$^{0/-}$ charge-state boundary, and a much longer screening tail associated with weak donor ionization in the neutral bulk. The resulting NV$^-$ depletion depth depends strongly on the nitrogen concentration but exhibits a more moderate dependence on boron doping. At $N_B = 10^{21}$ cm$^{-3}$, varying the interface grading scale $w$ from 0.5 to 8 nm changes the depletion depth by approximately 22 nm, whereas variations in the modeled bulk BDD charge response produce a shift of only 1.27 nm. These results indicate that, under the conditions studied, the nitrogen donor concentration and local interface structure primarily govern the equilibrium NV charge-state profile, rather than the bulk electronic response of BDD alone.

title: Second Harmonic Flexoelectricity
summary: Flexoelectricity (polarization induced by strain gradients) is assumed to be insensitive to space inversion in all materials: flexoelectric polarization should not depend on whether a crystal is bent upwards or downwards. In this work, we show that this assumption is wrong for ferroelectrics of all thickness and at all curvatures, owing to an intrinsic quadratic contribution that persists down to strain gradients of 1 m-1 or less, which is millions of times smaller than conventional expectations for nonlinear flexoelectricity. As a consequence, ferroelectric crystals can generate second-harmonic voltage at twice the oscillation frequency of the bending.

title: Swift Heavy Ion Tracks in Polymorphs of Titanium Dioxide: The Effects of Electron Beam and Crystal Structures
summary: Swift heavy ion (SHI) irradiation generates nanoscale damage in materials, offering opportunities for controlled modification of structural properties. Understanding the fundamental processes governing damage formation in altered regions remains a longstanding challenge. This work explores how crystal structure influences swift heavy ion-induced damage formation and evolution in rutile and anatase TiO2. Combining transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and molecular dynamics simulations, we investigate how differences in atomic arrangement govern track morphology and structural recovery. Although irradiation produces amorphous tracks in both polymorphs, their morphologies differ considerably. In rutile, tracks develop pronounced diameter variations, forming hourglass-like structures, whereas in anatase they retain a relatively uniform cylindrical shape. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that these differences arise from the distinct recrystallization behavior of the two crystal structures during rapid cooling, leading to different pathways of track evolution and recovery. Particular attention is paid to electron beam induced effects during TEM characterization, which can substantially modify the structure and apparent morphology of ion tracks. Prolonged electron beam exposure promotes the recrystallization of initially amorphous tracks and surface hillocks, accompanied by the development of Fresnel contrast. These findings highlight the importance of understanding beam-induced transformations for the reliable interpretation of TEM observations of radiation-damaged materials.

title: Supercell periodicity biases octahedral tilting and energetics in high-entropy perovskite oxides
summary: Odd-period supercells such as $3 \times 3 \times 5$ are often used for equimolar five-component compositions in computational studies of high-entropy perovskite oxides (HEPOs). However, such cells are known to constrain octahedral tilting because they cannot accommodate all standard tilt patterns (Glazer tilt systems). How strongly this constraint affects HEPOs, whose octahedra respond to local cation environments, remains unclear. Here we show that supercell periodicity systematically biases computed octahedral tilting and energetics. Using a machine-learning interatomic potential, we compared odd-period and tilt-commensurate cells for 13 HEPOs. Odd-period cells yielded smaller and less coherent tilts and higher energies, even after configurational averaging. In ~1,700-atom cells, tilt differences persisted in all compositions and energy differences in most. The bias extended to defects, with lower oxygen vacancy formation energies in odd-period cells for strongly tilted compositions. Based on these findings, a simple design rule for equimolar supercells is proposed to lift this constraint.

title: Mapping phase competition in GaAs under pressure and temperature
summary: Pressure-induced transformations in GaAs offer a means to investigate the interplay between crystal structure, electronic behaviour, and phase stability in a technologically important III-V semiconductor. Here, we have used structure search algorithm combined with first-principles calculations and identified high-pressure competitive phases. The previously proposed $Imm2$ structure lies above the calculated minimum-enthalpy envelope. The static enthalpy calculations with the PBEsol functional predict the transition sequence $F\bar{4}3m \rightarrow Cmcm \rightarrow I\bar{4}m2 \rightarrow C2/m \rightarrow Amm2$, at approximately 12, 14, 34, and 69 GPa, respectively. The initial zinc blende to $Cmcm$ transition is accompanied by a volume reduction of approximately 17.5 % and metallization within the PBEsol description. Phonon calculations support the dynamical stability of all five phases at representative pressures, while elastic calculations characterize their mechanical response. Vibrational free energies are incorporated within the quasiharmonic approximation to examine phase competition over 0-80 GPa and 0-1000 K. These results identify competing high-pressure structures and connect their relative energetics with the electronic, vibrational, and elastic responses of compressed GaAs.

title: Assessment of electric-field-induced forces for bulk solids within the projector-augmented wave method
summary: We assess the performance of electric-field-induced forces for bulk solids within the projector-augmented wave method. This capability allows for first-principles structural relaxations of bulk semiconductors and insulators under external electric fields, thereby enabling the calculation of linear and nonlinear responses to electric fields as well as properties associated with electric-field-driven structural changes. The approach is first validated by presenting calculated ion-clamped and unclamped dielectric and piezoelectric constants, quadratic dielectric susceptibilities, and Born effective charges for semiconductors AlX (X=P, As and Sb), showing good agreement with density functional perturbation theory calculations as well as with available experimental and theoretical data. As a further demonstration, we examine the electric-field-driven antiferroelectric-to-ferroelectric phase transition in AgNbO$_3$, for which our computed polarization versus electric field hysteresis loop aligns with previous calculations.

title: Magnetic History and Field Sweep Rate Effects on Transformation Hysteresis in $\mathrm{Ni}_{41}\mathrm{Co}_{9}\mathrm{Mn}_{31.5}\mathrm{Ga}_{18.5}$
summary: Hysteresis in magnetic-field-induced structural phase transformations is a major obstacle to the application of metamagnetic shape memory alloys. One promising approach to reduce hysteresis is to utilize a metastable martensitic state generated by magnetic-field cycling. However, the mechanism by which the metastable state reduces hysteresis remains unclear. Here, microsecond pulsed-field magnetization measurements are used to investigate the transformation kinetics of $\mathrm{Ni}_{41}\mathrm{Co}_{9}\mathrm{Mn}_{31.5}\mathrm{Ga}_{18.5}$. Magnetic-field cycling reduces the hysteresis width by approximately 50-60%, demonstrating that substantial suppression persists on a microsecond timescale. Comparison with millisecond pulsed-field measurements suggests that the reverse martensitic transformation field is more sensitive to the field sweep rate for the metastable martensite than for the initial martensite. Possible explanations include enhanced thermal activation associated with a lower effective activation barrier and differences in the athermal contribution arising from different metastable martensitic microstructures.

title: Efficient Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
summary: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) reach an accuracy close to quantum mechanical reference calculations at a small fraction of the cost. Efficiency is the purpose of MLIPs, yet strategies for efficient MLIPs have not been reviewed systematically. This review takes efficiency as its guideline. To compare MLIPs on a common footing, we represent them in a complete basis expansion, the Atomic Cluster Expansion (ACE) and its graph generalization (GRACE). The expansion is canonical, built from products of single-particle functions. Classical interatomic potentials, such as the embedded-atom method, and many modern MLIPs, including equivariant transformers, can be represented within this expansion. Much of the apparent diversity of MLIP architectures therefore reflects how non-linearity, layer coupling and optimization are handled rather than which interactions the models can represent. We show how the cost of an MLIP becomes linear in system size and, at fixed rank of the tensor decomposition, in model complexity, and we discuss the role of machine learning, which provides non-linear parameterizations and optimization. Because efficiency is meaningful only at a given accuracy, we also compare accuracy and cost. On the Matbench Discovery leaderboard, models with three to five layers approach the accuracy of deeper models, and one basis, truncated along the Pareto front of error and speed, spans more than two orders of magnitude in cost. Ultimately, training data determine the quality of any MLIP.

title: Burgers vectors from Voronoi topology
summary: Automated dislocation analysis is standard in atomistic simulations, yet current tools are limited to a handful of crystal structures. We introduce an algorithm without adjustable parameters, based on Voronoi topology, that identifies dislocations in a broad class of crystals. Each face shared by two cells that match the ideal crystal is taken as a step in it, and summing these steps around closed circuits of such cells yields exact Burgers vectors, without geometric templates. Tested on dislocations inserted into all 9,610 Materials Project structures whose Voronoi cells are stable with a wide margin, the algorithm finds every dislocation with its correct Burgers vector. In raw molecular-dynamics snapshots, including eleven dislocation types in $\theta$-Al$_2$Cu and bcc iron up to its melting point, every Burgers vector it returns is correct, although near melting the dislocations merge into one cluster. Voronoi topology thus provides a natural language in which a crystal, its defects, and their Burgers vectors are all described.

title: Combined magnetic and structural transition state in first-principles calculations
summary: We present a generalized nudged elastic band (NEB) implementation within potential-based constrained density-functional theory (cDFT) for calculating transition pathways that simultaneously optimize atomic, lattice, and magnetic degrees of freedom. Unlike standard fixed-cell NEB calculations restricted to atomic displacements, our framework consistently couples atomic forces, stresses, and spin torques. The method supports fixed- and variable-cell approaches for collinear and non- collinear magnetic configurations, by incorporating magnetic torques and generalized cell coordinates within the NEB optimization. To validate the methodology, we present benchmark calculations for representative magnetostructural systems. Specifically, we investigate the bcc-to-hcp transformation in Fe and the antiferromagnetic-to-ferromagnetic transition in FeRh using the variable-cell formalism. Furthermore, we examine spin-reversal processes in two-dimensional CrI3 to analyze the influence of spin-orbit coupling on transition paths and their associated energy barriers.

title: Koopmans spectral functionals for excitons in materials
summary: Accurate first-principles characterization of excitons typically relies on the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) combined with quasiparticle energies from computationally demanding GW calculations. Here, we replace the GW step with quasiparticle energies from Koopmans-compliant spectral functionals, an approach we call BSE@qKI, and implement it in an automated, reproducible AiiDA workflow. For a set of benchmark semiconductors, BSE@qKI reproduces experimental band gaps and first exciton energies with mean absolute relative errors of 13% and 4%, respectively, comparable to BSE@G0W0 for the gaps and markedly better for the excitation energies. We also apply the method to the layered magnetic semiconductor CrI3, obtaining an absorption spectrum that reproduces the main experimental features. These results establish BSE@qKI as a GW-free alternative to BSE@G0W0 for systematic studies of excitonic properties in complex materials.

title: Solvent/Antisolvent-Driven Etching of 2D Layered Halide Perovskite Microcrystals toward Endo-Epitaxial Heterostructures
summary: Engineering internal interfaces within single crystals remains challenging, particularly in soft ionic materials such as layered halide perovskites (LHPs), for which conventional lithographic approaches are difficult to implement. Here we report a solvent/antisolvent-driven strategy for controlled etching of LHP microcrystals, producing well-defined rectangular cavities. Etching initiates at the top surface and proceeds preferentially along the crystallographic [100] and [010] directions. Cavity dimensions are tuned through etching time, temperature and etchant composition. The reaction can be interrupted and resumed, enabling stepwise cavity evolution through successive etching cycles. The resulting cavities serve as confined templates for regrowth of compositionally distinct LHPs, yielding endo-epitaxial heterostructures with designed internal architectures. The approach extends across diverse LHP compositions and antisolvent systems, while sequential precursor addition controls the extent of internal regrowth. This strategy establishes a route to engineering internal heterointerfaces in single-crystal perovskites through controlled chemical etching and confined growth.

title: First-order correction to the self-consistent harmonic approximation free energy: Impact on the negative thermal expansion and phonon dynamics in ScF$_3$
summary: Strongly anharmonic crystals are often treated using the self-consistent harmonic approximation with variationally optimized Gaussian density matrices or the related self-consistent phonon theory. Both approaches capture substantial phonon renormalization but exclude connected non-Gaussian free-energy correlations. Here, we derive the first-order post-variational correction generated by the lowest non-vanishing normal-ordered residual vertex. Normal ordering the residual interaction around the optimized state shows that the linear and quadratic vertices vanish at the stationary variational solution, leaving a fluctuation-dressed cubic interaction whose second-order vacuum and two-point contractions generate the free-energy correction and the dynamical bubble self-energy, respectively. In ScF$_3$, the variational optimization on the full Born-Oppenheimer potential accounts for most of the shift in the thermal-expansion crossover temperature between negative and positive values relative to self-consistent phonon theory with a fourth-order potential. The connected correction changes the crossover modestly, but its volume derivative appreciably shifts the pressure-remapped cubic local-stability limit. Using the bare cubic vertex appears to improve agreement with the thermodynamic measurements, yet it systematically underestimates the measured zone-boundary tilt-mode energies at high temperatures. The fluctuation-dressed interaction gives more moderate thermodynamic corrections but yields phonon energies in better agreement with experiments. These results show that connected non-Gaussian correlations can significantly affect free-energy derivatives and soft-mode dynamics near a structural instability, and identify the optimized Gaussian state as the natural reference for constructing residual interactions beyond the stochastic self-consistent harmonic approximation.

title: Targeted material doping to enable the formation and coherent propagation of Laser Induced Periodic Surface Structures (LIPSS): the ZnO paradigm
summary: This work explores how the initial free carrier density governs the formation and coherent propagation of Low Spatial Frequency Laser-Induced Periodic Surface Structures (LSF-LIPSS). As a paradigm we have analyzed the behavior of ad-hoc-doped ZnO films. ZnO is a multifunctional Transparent Conducting Oxide (TCO) with many scientific and technologic uses including applications in biomedicine, photonics, sensing or photocatalysis. Many of them would benefit from the use of large area, electrically anisotropic surfaces. By introducing small amounts of Yb3+ as donor dopant in ZnO films grown by Pulse Laser Deposition (PLD), we have substantially improved its carrier density at room temperature (RT) and its electrical conductivity while preserving the functional properties of pure ZnO. For RT carrier densities ne > 1019 cm-3, coherent propagation of LSF-LIPSS has been successfully achieved upon irradiation with 350 fs laser pulses at 1030 nm at high repetition rate (500 kHz) and for laser scanning speeds well above 1 m/s. However, the ablation mechanism (ZnO sublimation at the LIPSS valleys) and the large melting temperature of ZnO, make the thermal conductivity of the substrate, the film thickness and the irradiation pulse duration to play a crucial role in determining the morphology of the LSF-LIPPS propagated over large areas, especially in avoiding film cracking. The results achieved upon optimization fully confirm the role of free carrier density in the large-scale propagation of high quality LSF-LIPSS in doped ZnO and enable using these structures to easily generate large electrical anisotropies over macroscopic regions with conductivities along the LIPSS several times larger than transversally.

title: Prior-guided adaptive local refinement of foundation interatomic potentials
summary: Foundation interatomic potentials enable simulations across diverse materials, but task-specific inaccuracies can require additional first-principles data. Obtaining these data is challenging when the relevant local environments arise in large simulation cells. Here we introduce the Prior-guided Adaptive Refinement Scheme (PARS), which identifies weakly supported environments during molecular dynamics by comparing their frozen representations with prototypes of pretraining environments, without requiring initial task labels or model ensembles. Selected environments are reconstructed as compact periodic cells for first-principles labelling and iterative refinement. Applications to phase stability, surface migration and vacancy clustering show improvements in target properties, including an 81% reduction in the mean absolute error of Ti vacancy-cluster energies per vacancy relative to the pretrained model. For Si/Ge, a foundation potential refined using 800 labelled cells containing 10-128 atoms is subsequently distilled into a compact potential without additional first-principles training labels. In simulations containing approximately 362,880 atoms, the distilled model predicts an interfacial thermal resistance consistent with that of a potential trained directly on density-functional theory data. These results demonstrate a route for adapting foundation potentials to target applications through local reference calculations.

title: VQkit: A Unified and Extensible Framework for VASP and Quantum ESPRESSO Pre- and Post-Processing
summary: VQkit is a Python-based computational toolkit developed to streamline the pre- and post-processing of density functional theory calculations performed using Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) and Quantum ESPRESSO (QE). The framework employs a unified representation of lattice vectors, atomic coordinates, chemical species, and positional constraints, enabling cross-code structure conversion, geometry manipulation, crystallographic reconstruction, and code-specific input generation. Its pre-processing capabilities include symmetry-dependent reciprocal-space path generation, atomic constraints, and automated preparation of simulation inputs. The post-processing framework provides calculation convergence inspection, extraction of total energies and Fermi levels, electronic band-structure and density-of-states analysis, orbital-resolved electronic-structure processing, charge-density analysis, and evaluation of application-specific materials properties. The computational implementation is evaluated through elastic-property benchmarks for HfC, ZrC, ZrO2, Ti, and diamond, showing close agreement between VQkit and VASPKIT for VASP-based calculations, with differences observed in the corresponding QE results. By integrating cross-code interoperability, automated simulation preparation, standardized post-processing, and quantitative property evaluation within a common computational environment, VQkit reduces workflow fragmentation and facilitates consistent pre- and post-processing of first-principles calculations.

title: Altermagnetism-induced magneto-optical effects
summary: Altermagnets break time-reversal symmetry despite their zero net magnetization, enabling time-reversal-odd responses while retaining the advantages of antiferromagnets. However, magneto-optical (MO) effects are not universal among altermagnets because MO effects typically arise from magnetic dipole order (ferromagnetism), which is generally absent in altermagnets. In this work, we address this limitation by establishing octupolar MO effects, which arise from magnetic octupole order through spatial dispersion. Owing to this distinct origin, octupolar MO effects do not necessarily require spin-orbit coupling even in collinear magnets and can arise without an external magnetic field in antiferromagnets where conventional MO effects are symmetry-forbidden. Such antiferromagnets include $d$-wave altermagnets such as RuO$_2$ and KV$_2$Se$_2$O, certain $g$- and $i$-wave altermagnets, including CrSb, as well as noncoplanar antiferromagnets such as MnTe$_2$ and pyrochlore iridates with all-in-all-out magnetic order. From an experimental perspective, octupolar MO effects can reach detectable magnitudes and offer potential for magnetic-domain imaging, as supported by numerical calculations showing $\mu$rad-scale Faraday rotation for a 100-nm-thick sample in the visible-light range and a sign reversal between opposite domains. Furthermore, octupolar MO effects are linked to an $f$-sum rule, enabling a quantitative estimate of the spin magnetic octupole moment from optical measurements. These results extend the scope of MO effects to a broad class of antiferromagnets, including altermagnets, and open a field-free optical route to exploring magnetic octupole order.

title: Interfacial electrostatics: From polar insulators to charged-layer metals
summary: Polar discontinuities are typically described as arising from charged atomic planes, a spontaneous polarization, or a combination, in insulating films interfaced with vacuum, nonpolar insulators or metals. The resulting electrostatics are well established for systems such as LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$, BaTiO$_3$/SrRuO$_3$, and BiFeO$_3$/SrRuO$_3$. However, recent observations of "polar-discontinuity-like" behavior at interfaces in which the metal contains formally charged layers (e.g., rare-earth nickelates) challenge this picture. In this work, we summarize the theoretical framework used to define and quantify interface charge, layer polarization, and screening in the three reference systems above, and then discuss signatures attributed to the formal-charge polar discontinuity arising when SmNiO$_3$, a metal with formally charged (001) layers, is interfaced with ferroelectric BaTiO$_3$. We show how concepts developed for polar discontinuities between two insulators and for screening at metallic interfaces can rationalize the reported effects and identify where our understanding of these systems leaves open questions.

title: Canonical spin glass behavior and memory effects in van der Waals magnet (Fe0.55Ni0.45)3GaTe2
summary: We demonstrate the canonical spin-glass behavior and non-equilibrium dynamics in a single-crystalline Ni-doped van der Waals magnet (Fe0.55Ni0.45)3GaTe2 with a freezing temperature $T_f \approx 45.5$ K from detailed ac susceptibility and dc magnetization measurements. The temperature-dependent dc magnetization exhibits strong magnetic irreversibility and the ac susceptibility shows that the peak at $T_f$ shifts towards higher temperatures with increase in ac frequency, indicating the presence of a spin glass state. The relative shift of the freezing temperature $\delta T_f$ per decade of frequency in ac susceptibility is estimated to be 0.0072. Dynamic scaling analysis of the frequency-dependent freezing temperature using the power law reveals the single spin flip relaxation time $\tau_0=2\times10^{-13}$ s and critical exponent $z\nu=8.1$, while the Vogel-Fulcher law yields Vogel-Fulcher temperature $T_0=43$ K and activation energy $E_a/k_B=81$ K with $E_a/k_BT_0=1.88$. The obtained values of these characteristic parameters lie well within the range associated with a canonical spin glass. The detailed non-equilibrium dynamics study, involving the magnetic relaxation and memory effect, further confirms the glassy behavior. The memory effect in zero-field-cooled magnetization establishes that the glassy state arises from the cooperative spin-spin interaction and not from superparamagnetism. The asymmetric response of magnetic relaxation with respect to negative and positive temperature cycle favors the hierarchical model of memory effects over the droplet model.

title: From a High-T$\rm_C$ Spin-Gapless Semiconductor to a Spin-Glass: The Role of Disorder in NiMnCrAl
summary: We combine first-principles calculations with structural, magnetic, and transport measurements to investigate the influence of chemical disorder on the quaternary Heusler alloy NiMnCrAl. For the ordered Y-type structure, density-functional-theory calculations predict a ferrimagnetic spin-gapless-semiconducting state with a total magnetic moment of $1.99\,\mu_{\mathrm{B}}/\mathrm{f.u.}$ and a mean-field ordering temperature of approximately $1300~\mathrm{K}$. Polycrystalline NiMnCrAl forms in a single average cubic phase; however, combined x-ray diffraction, neutron diffraction, and extended x-ray absorption fine-structure measurements reveal substantial antisite disorder, characterized by predominantly B2-like disorder with additional cross-sublattice mixing. No long-range ferrimagnetic transition is observed up to $700~\mathrm{K}$. Instead, the compound exhibits a broad magnetic anomaly near $37~\mathrm{K}$, frequency-dependent ac susceptibility, slow stretched-exponential relaxation, and field-cooled and zero-field-cooled memory effects, establishing a glassy magnetic state. The electrical resistivity is metallic and the Seebeck coefficient is negative, consistent with the loss of the ideal spin-gapless electronic structure. Exchange-interaction calculations show that antisite disorder introduces short Mn--Mn separations and competing antiferromagnetic Mn--Mn and Mn--Cr interactions, providing a microscopic basis for magnetic frustration. These results demonstrate the strong sensitivity to the predicted spin-gapless and ferrimagnetic states of NiMnCrAl to chemical disorder.

title: Mechanically induced self-propagating reactions within the realm of mechanochemistry: Fundamentals, overview, in situ monitoring and perspectives
summary: Mechanically induced self-propagating reaction (MSR) represents a promising but rather underexplored phenomenon within mechanochemistry, a solvent-free alternative to classical solution-based chemistry. In contrast to the gradual mechanochemical reactions, MSRs are sub-second combustive-like processes bringing about substantial benefits such as faster product formation, time efficiency, and lower energy consumption. Despite the fact that the mechanochemical field is in the research spotlight, MSR investigation remains on the periphery. This review aims to catalyze a renaissance in MSR fundamentals investigation by reviewing the current state-of-the-art. This is done via systematically reviewing the reaction systems that were reported to react via a MSR in the past twenty years, such as metal-metalloid ones (carbides, borides, silicides, and carbonitrides), metal chalcogenides, metal oxides, and other specific types of reactions. A couple of case studies are briefly reviewed for each system, and the comprehensive table follows afterward. The review also revisits the factors impacting the MSR course from milling conditions and reagent's properties point of view, showing either a direct or inverse relationship with MSR ignition time. The recent development in the in situ monitoring of mechanochemical reactions allowed to obtain some mechanistic insights into the MSR process, which are summarized in the last chapter.

title: AlCoCuFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Nanoparticle Melting and Solidification: A Classical Molecular Dynamics Simulation Study
summary: The processes of melting and solidification of an AlCoCuFeNi high-entropy alloy nanoparticle with a diameter of about 10 nm were studied by classical molecular dynamics simulation using an embedded atom model potential. Three cooling rates, 10^11, 10^12, and 10^13 K/s, were considered. Melting and crystallization behavior were characterized through the temperature dependence of the potential energy. Structural evolution was analyzed using adaptive common-neighbor analysis (CNA) and radial distribution functions (RDF). The results show that the final structure changes from amorphous to crystalline as the cooling rate decreases. A pronounced temperature hysteresis associated with melting and crystallization was also observed.

title: Engineering antiferromagnetic (LaVO3)m/(PrVO3)n superlattices
summary: In this study, we demonstrate the atomic-scale engineering of antiferromagnetic (LaVO3)m/(PrVO3)n superlattices grown by MBE on (001)-oriented SrTiO3 substrates. Our work achieved a precise layer-by-layer control, revealing how interface-driven structural distortions can be systematically tuned. X-ray diffraction and reciprocal space mapping confirm both the epitaxial strain state and the high crystalline quality of the superlattices. High-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy further uncovers layer-resolved atomic displacements, where La3+ and Pr3+ exhibit antipolar motions modulated by the superlattice periodicity. The alternate stackings of LaVO3 and PrVO3 yield a unique antiferromagnetic transition temperature, which can be tuned by adjusting their relative proportions. This behavior exists despite the distinct spin ordering temperatures observed in the constituent materials. Layer-resolved spectroscopic measurements reveal that the hybridization of La and Pr 5d orbitals with O 2p orbitals is also modulated and directly correlated to the oxygen octahedra rotations. By determining the orbital hybridization and mapping the cation displacements as proxies, we can visualize indirectly the trilinear coupling between oxygen octahedra rotations and antipolar rare earth displacements. Notably, the interfacial oxygen octahedra connectivity between cubic SrTiO3 substrate and orthorhombic vanadate layers significantly influences the structural distortions. These distortions, almost quenched near the interface, relax over few unit cells, demonstrating how strain and interfacial effects propagate through the superlattice. This study illustrates how artificial superlattices can be engineered to control structural distortions at the atomic scale, offering a pathway to tune the magnetic properties through strain-distortion relationships in perovskite oxides.

title: Engineering third order absorbing exceptional points in multi-drive cavity magnonics for enhanced sensing
summary: We consider a four mode cavity magnonics system consisting of two coupled resonators containing a pair of YIG spheres. Each resonator has two input-output ports allowing for the application of multiple drive fields. We show that with control of the dipolar coupling strength between the YIG spheres the relative amplitude and phase of the drive fields can be used to tune the system to third order absorbing exceptional points. The system considered here offers considerable flexibility and may be useful for high sensitivity detection as absorbing exceptional points can avoid the eigenbasis collapse associated with their resonant counterparts.

title: From quasiperiodic three-colour order on a triangular lattice to covalent carbon sheets
summary: Can the quasiperiodic colouring of a lattice be encoded in the bonds of a single carbon sheet? We construct golden-, silver- and bronze-mean three-colour patterns on a triangular lattice. The positions of one colour determine the other two through a nearest-neighbour rule. The three patterns have eight, nine and seven first-shell environments, respectively. A triangle of three identical motifs frustrates the alternating bond ports of each of the three molecular alphabets in the golden and silver patterns. The bronze pattern admits four designs with direct or ethynylene connections. Three periodic structures reproduce its infinite environment frequencies in a local-energy model. For a 708-atom sheet with independently matched environment counts, the predicted energy lies 0.295 meV per carbon below the density-functional result. Across four periodic cells initialized from two smaller donors, relaxation changes the bond lengths by at most 0.00113 angstroms in root-mean-square terms. Fitting one 60-degree sector to relaxed periodic geometries gives complete sixfold-symmetric fragments with up to 22,140 carbon atoms. In the 13,950-atom directly linked sheet, a $\pi$ doublet places 79.05% of its weight in a boundary shell comprising 7.96% of the atoms, whereas the lowest unoccupied doublet places only 0.124% there. These calculations connect a testable motif-selection rule to the energetics and finite-patch spectra of candidate quasiperiodic carbon sheets.

title: Spin and Orbital Angular Momentum Textures at Chiral Molecule-Metal Interfaces
summary: Chiral molecular adsorption can modify the spin and orbital character of metal surface states, providing an electronic-structure basis for interpreting spin-dependent interfacial phenomena. Using first-principles calculations with spin-orbit coupling, band unfolding, and an atom-projected orbital angular momentum (OAM) analysis, we investigate spin and OAM textures at chiral heptahelicene/Au(111) interfaces and compare them with clean Au (111) and an achiral coronene/Au system. Adsorption changes the orientations of the spin and OAM vectors and reduces the sampled OAM magnitudes of Au-derived surface states near the Fermi level. The two heptahelicene enantiomers exhibit textures related by mirror and time-reversal symmetries, whereas the comparison with coronene identifies changes that also occur without molecular chirality. These results clarify how molecular adsorption modifies interfacial spin and orbital character and establish symmetry constraints relevant to chirality-dependent photoemission.

title: Charge-transfer excitation drives cooperative phonon-assisted exciton self-trapping in NiPS$_3$
summary: Carrier self-trapping is a fundamental relaxation pathway in strongly correlated quantum materials, yet the microscopic lattice motions that drive it have remained largely inaccessible to direct observation. Here we investigate the van der Waals antiferromagnet NiPS$_3$ upon excitation across its ligand-to-metal charge-transfer gap, and reveal a nonequilibrium pathway that initially generates unbound carriers before they evolve into correlated excitonic states. Using ultrabroadband optical-pump terahertz-probe spectroscopy, we simultaneously track carrier localization and the associated lattice dynamics in real time. The transient conductive response quenches with a time constant of $\sim$109 fs and evolves into a localized exciton state, accompanied by pronounced renormalization of Ni-S optical phonons and the emergence of a transient 2.7 THz vibrational mode. Temperature-dependent measurements, together with mode-resolved dielectric dynamics and symmetry analysis, identify the 2.7 and 8.0 THz responses as spectroscopic indicators of exciton self-trapping and point to a cooperative two-phonon mechanism. These findings establish the excitation pathway as a key parameter controlling carrier localization and many-body relaxation in strongly coupled quantum materials.

title: Localized corrosion resistance of ultrafine-grained austenitic steel 321 obtained by Rotary Swaging: The role of annealing conditions
summary: The object of this study was austenitic steel 321, which has an ultrafine-grained (UFG) structure formed by Rotary Swaging (RS). RS leads to the formation of a two-phase macroscopically heterogeneous and, at the same time, a microscopically homogeneous UFG structure with an increased content of martensite. It has been shown that secondary TiC nanoparticles form in the annealing at 450-550C, the reverse transformation of martensite into austenite occurs at 550-650C, and recrystallization begins at 700C. Electrochemical studies of the resistance of the UFG steel to general corrosion, intergranular corrosion (IGC), and pitting corrosion (PC) have been carried out. It has been shown that the UFG steel after RS has a reduced IGC resistance. The surface of steel rods after RS has a reduced hardness and corrosion resistance compared to the central part of the rods. It has been shown that in the temperature range of 450-550C, there is a slight increase in the microhardness, and a significant decrease in the IGC and PC resistance of the UFG steel. Recrystallization at 700-800C leads to an increased PC resistance and IGC resistance. Annealing conditions have been determined that ensure a good combination of strength, ductility and corrosion resistance of the UFG steel. It was demonstrated that to explain the non-monotonic variation in the localized corrosion rate of UFG steel during annealing, it is necessary to consider not only the well-known effects of martensite and delta-ferrite, but also the precipitation of TiC particles and the changes in the free energy of non-equilibrium grain boundaries.
