title: Effect of superplastic deformation on the intergranular corrosion resistance of austenitic steel 321 with different types of UFG structure: A case of homogeneous and heterogeneous microstructure obtained by ECAP
summary: The effects of superplasticity (SP) on the structure, hardness, and intergranular corrosion (IGC) resistance of UFG 321L steel are reported. By increasing the number of the ECAP cycles (N) and varying the ECAP temperature, and annealing temperature, the degree of the microstructural heterogeneity was changed. Regardless of the microstructural homogeneity degree, UFG steels demonstrated the possibility of realizing the SP effect at temperatures below the onset temperature of dynamic recrystallization. The dependence of ductility of the UFG steel on the test temperature is non-monotonic with a minimum at 450-600C. The maximum elongation to failure (~250%) was achieved at a SP temperature of 800C. The SP deformation of the UFG steel is controlled by the power law creep. It is shown that the hardness of UFG steel samples after SP is equal than the hardness of UFG steels annealed at the same temperature. It is also shown what SP leads to a decrease in the IGC resistance of the UFG steel. Heterostructured steel have reduced ductility, as well as lower resistance to IGC after tension tests at room temperature (RT). The minimum IGC resistance is ensured at N=2, and the maximum - at N=4. The IGC resistance of homogeneous UFG samples after tension testing exceeds the IGC resistance of coarse-grained steel. Tension test at a RT has the greatest negative effect on the IGC resistance of heterostructured steel, and the least negative effect on the IGC resistance of homogeneous steel. Increasing the number of ECAP cycles enhances the ductility of the UFG steel at 750-900C. Increasing the ECAP temperature results in a simultaneous decrease in ductility and flow stress. Heterostructured steel exhibits minimal values of the activation energy of SP deformation. Increasing the number of ECAP cycles and increasing the ECAP temperature lead to an increase in the activation energy of SP deformation.

title: Probing Phase Fluctuations in Cuprates by Multidimensional Josephson Spectroscopy
summary: The normal state of cuprate superconductors is believed to host precursor electron pairing above the superconducting transition temperature. These pre-formed pairs, which extend over an unknown temperature range, are expected to lack long-range phase coherence. Because spectroscopic evidence for this hypothesis is only indirect, new methods to probe these physics are needed. Nonlinear terahertz spectroscopy allows one to probe high-order time correlation functions and is therefore sensitive to fluctuations. Measurements of third-harmonic generation along the superconducting planes have revealed responses persisting above Tc, but a clear relation between these optical responses and specific properties of the fluctuating state has not yet been established. Here, we apply angle-resolved multidimensional terahertz spectroscopy to probe the optical nonlinearity of the Josephson tunneling resonance in La1.83Sr0.17CuO4 across the superconducting to normal state transition. We find that among all third-order nonlinear responses, the non-rephasing multidimensional signal is especially sensitive to non-mean field fluctuations of the order parameter. We measure a crossover occurring at T ~ Tc between a mean-field optical nonlinearity that dominates at low temperatures and one that is mediated by short-range superconducting fluctuations. We present a theoretical framework that connects the out-of-plane optical response in both regimes to the fluctuating in-plane superconducting state, and contrast the sensitivity of different types of terahertz nonlinearities to fluctuating order.

title: Symmetry-reduced k-point sampling and Wannier analysis with localized Gaussian orbitals
summary: Brillouin-zone sampling with localized orbitals requires consistent transformations between sparse real-space matrices and complex Bloch states. Symmetry reduces the number of reciprocal-space problems, but scalar integration weights alone cannot reconstruct the matrices and wavefunctions needed for densities and orbital analysis. We develop a unified formulation of these transformations for nonorthogonal Gaussian bases and describe its implementation in CP2K. Atom permutations, local orbital rotations, and lattice phases connect irreducible-point solutions to full symmetry orbits while preserving the overlap metric. Direct and fast lattice transforms couple this construction to self-consistent calculations, including complex orbital optimization and finite-temperature occupations. Gauge-consistent full-mesh orbitals and directed inter-point overlaps support Wannier90 export, Wannier construction, and Hamiltonian interpolation. In silicon and aluminium tests, symmetry reduces a 64-point mesh to four representatives while retaining cell energies or electronic free energies within $1.5\times10^{-12}$ hartree of the unreduced calculation. Hybrid exchange and many-body applications illustrate the additional role of auxiliary bases and transfer momenta. The resulting framework connects symmetry-reduced integration to gauge-consistent analysis of periodic electronic states within a localized-orbital representation.

title: Orbital differentiation in a rare earth ion near half filling
summary: In the electronic structure of rare earth ions, details can be crucial for understanding the origin of correlated states. Currently, state-of-the-art wavefunction-based methods (e.g. CASSCF) can capture single-ion properties of molecular magnets and some band insulating systems, but are expensive to perform, and cannot be applied to metallic systems. Here, we carry out full multiplet calculations for SmN with the cubic rock-salt structure using the crystal field software Quanty. The calculated experimental observables from our model agree precisely with magnetic susceptibility and inelastic neutron scattering experiments, and the spatially resolved spin density also agrees with DFT predictions. By tuning the crystal field parameters, our full multiplet-derived wavefunctions reveal the presence of orbital differentiation of the ground $J=\frac{5}{2}$ manifold into two groups, which are distinct subspaces with different orbital stiffness. This violation of Hund's rule, observed with a fast and inexpensive calculation tool, represents a step forward for microscopic models of rare earth materials, and may provide support for the claim of unconventional triplet superconductivity in SmN.

title: Domain walls of a spin-chirality ferroelectric as tunable quantum particles
summary: In frustrated spin chains with competing nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor exchange, the vector spin chirality sets the electric polarization, so a ferroelectric domain wall is a domain wall of the chirality. The semiclassical picture suggests nonlocal switching dynamics due to topological constraints on the spins, but little is known about such domain walls in a quantum spin chain. Using density-matrix renormalization group calculations for a frustrated spin-1/2 XXZ chain in which a bond alternation $\delta$ opens a spin gap, we show that the wall then becomes a quantum particle. In a finite chain, it has the energy levels and wave functions of a particle in a box, and it moves under an electric field as a particle under a constant force does. In the infinite chain, its mass grows by more than two orders of magnitude as $\delta$ decreases and diverges at $\delta^*\approx0.012$, where the bottom of its band becomes flat; below $\delta^*$ the band has two degenerate minima away from its center. The large mass results from a near cancellation of in-plane and out-of-plane exchange energies.

title: Quantum Interband-Coherence-Driven Inverse Faraday Effect in Intrinsic Graphene
summary: The inverse Faraday effect converts the angular momentum of circularly polarized light into a quasistatic magnetization, providing a fundamental route to ultrafast optical control of magnetic fields. We develop an analytical quantum theory of this effect in intrinsic graphene, where massless Dirac fermions, electron-hole symmetry, and weak spin-orbit coupling suppress conventional population-based interpretations. We show that in intrinsic graphene, the helicity-dependent orbital magnetization arises from the off-diagonal zero-harmonic component of the second-order density matrix, rather than from intraband carrier circulation or diagonal population imbalance. We obtain closed expressions for the induced temporal surface magnetization, its finite-pulse dynamics, and the nonlocal stray magnetic field generated by the two-dimensional (2D) source. Optical helicity, frequency, pulse envelope, and beam profile independently control the response. Our results identify intrinsic graphene as an ideal platform for coherent orbital optomagnetism in 2D Dirac matter.

title: Thermal radiation of nanowires and near-field interaction with substrates: exact computation and proximity approximation
summary: Radiative heat transfer involving complex nano-objects is difficult to evaluate due to their sub-wavelength size, which induces deviation to macroscopic Planck's opaque surface-to-surface formalism, and due to the small distances involved, which lead to near-field radiative (photon tunneling) effects. As a result, thermal radiation has mostly been neglected in analyses of thermal transport in nanowires. Here, we report on calculations of thermal emission by single nanowires and on the radiative interaction between suspended silicon nanowires and flat substrates. We observe that metallic nanowires can be particularly emissive in comparison to wires made of other materials. While thermal emission from an isolated silicon nanowire is lower than Stefan-Boltzmann's prediction, the radiative exchange with a substrate can be larger by one order of magnitude. The considered configurations also allow benchmarking various levels of common or original approximations, including, in near field, the proximity approximation, the thickness-dependent PA, the electrostatic approach, and the effective emissivity in the far field.

title: The SymTFT and Quantum Phases of Matter
summary: The symmetry topological field theory (SymTFT) provides a unified framework for ordinary and generalized symmetries of quantum many-body systems. By encoding symmetry in a topological theory in one higher dimension, it separates symmetry data from the details of a specific quantum system. In this review, we give a pedagogical introduction to this framework and survey its applications to phases of quantum matter. For fusion category symmetries in ${(1+1)}$d, we explain how the SymTFT characterizes anomalies, classifies gapped phases, and organizes the symmetry structure of gapless phases. We also give a broad overview of further developments of this framework, including extensions to symmetries in higher dimensions, continuous symmetries, fermionic systems, mixed states, and spacetime symmetries.

title: Constraints on the volume enclosed by Fermi surfaces
summary: A fundamental property of a Fermi liquid (FL) is that the volume enclosed by the Fermi surface is determined by $\rho$, the total density of electrons. In a fractionalized Fermi liquid (FL*), the volume enclosed by the Fermi surface is determined by the same expression after $\rho$ has been shifted by a quantized amount, most commonly to $\rho -1$ (we assume spin rotation invariance, for simplicity). The FL* shift is related to the quantized symmetry fractionalization data of a quantum spin liquid, whose fractionalized spinon excitations are present alongside the Fermi surface quasiparticles. In this review article, we establish the FL* Fermi volume by generalizing the original Luttinger proof for FL to parton gauge theories of the quantum spin liquid and FL*. We also discuss Oshikawa's flux insertion arguments for FL, and their extension to FL*, including a discussion of gapless spin liquids.

title: Tunable Topological Charge Order in Magnetic Moir\'e Systems
summary: Two-dimensional electrons in a strong magnetic field exhibit two seemingly incompatible ground states: incompressible quantum Hall liquids with a quantized Hall conductance, and electron crystals in which interactions drive the charge into ordered patterns. Moir\'e superlattices in transition-metal-dichalcogenide bilayers offer a tunable arena for this competition. Using neural quantum states (NQS) together with several methodological advances, we show how this competition unfolds. In particular, we demonstrate that the two end points are separated by an extended regime in which molecular charge order coexists with a quantized Hall response. We map the ground-state phase diagram of electrons at Landau-level filling $\nu_B=1$ in the presence of a moir\'e superlattice potential, with three electrons per moir\'e cell. In the deep triangular potential limit, the electrons form the topologically trivial "Wigner molecular crystal'' of three-electron artificial atoms, a state recently imaged at zero magnetic field in moir\'e bilayers. As the potential depth is lowered, molecular charge order remains while quantized Hall response emerges. At the honeycomb point, where each cell contains three electrons and two degenerate moir\'e minima, wells are either singly or doubly occupied and the doublons provide an emergent Ising degree of freedom. Starting from modest interaction strength, we find short-range doublon correlations within the Chern insulator which grow with interaction strength and eventually break sublattice symmetry, forming a N\'eel CDW with long-range order between doublons. The topological molecular regime lies at twist angles and magnetic fields directly accessible to current experiments. The methodological advances presented provide a scalable framework for exploring a broad range of questions in correlated quantum matter in the presence of magnetic fields.

title: Coexisting orders and dipolar Luttinger liquids in $\mathbb{Z}_N$ quantum torus chain
summary: We establish a unified ground-state phase diagram for the one-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_N$ quantum torus chain, which is connected to dipolar cluster and dipolar Ising chains via noninvertible dualities. Combining tensor-network calculations with bosonization and perturbation theory, we establish a rich phase diagram governed by the local Hilbert-space dimension $N$ and its parity. We identify phases with coexisting $X$ and $Z$ long-range orders ($C$ phase), and dipolar Luttinger liquids (dLL$_{\rm I}$ and dLL$_{\rm II}$) separating coexisting phases from single-order phases. Gapless dipolar excitations coexist with long-range order in dLLs. Both the $C$ and dLL phases appear at $N \geq 5$, but only the $C$ phases persist as $N\to \infty$. The stability of the dLL phase is understood by an emergent Luttinger liquid theory, with Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transitions out of it driven by competing umklapp and clock anisotropy perturbations. For odd $N \geq 5$, a third dLL phase (dLL$_{\rm III}$) emerges near $\theta = \pi$ due to the low-energy dynamics inside the exponentially degenerate ground-state manifold that maps onto an effective XXZ chain. Duality considerations suggest a possible gapless dipolar symmetry-protected topological phase and spontaneous dipole-symmetry breaking in dipolar cluster chains.

title: Preformed excitons in the excitonic density-wave state of monolayer 1$T'$-MoTe$_2$
summary: Phase-incoherent preformed excitons have long been anticipated in excitonic insulators, yet their characteristic signatures and underlying physics remain elusive, as the electrical neutrality of excitons hinders direct probes of condensate phase coherence. Here we exploit the emergent excitonic density wave driven by phase-coherent pairings in systems hosting momentum-separated electron and hole Fermi pockets, such as monolayer 1$T'$-MoTe$_2$, as an experimentally accessible probe of excitonic phase coherence. We observe in 1$T'$-MoTe$_2$ that the density-wave order and its associated emergent collective excitations, as revealed by Raman spectroscopy, vanish above $T_c\approx80~$K, whereas the excitonic-insulator state, characterized by a single-particle gap in transport and tunneling measurements, persists up to $T_g\approx100~$K, revealing an intermediate pseudogap-like regime of preformed excitons without long-range phase coherence. Theoretically, we attribute this intriguing separation to two distinct processes governing the loss of excitonic order by its own emergent excitations: boson-driven phase decoherence and fermion-driven pair breaking. Specifically, we identify an emergent low-lying collective excitation as a lattice-pinned phason (phase mode), whose heating-induced gap softening enhances phase fluctuations and drives condensate phase decoherence above $T_c$, while thermal excitations of fermionic quasiparticles gradually suppress and ultimately destroy pairing amplitude at the higher $T_g$. The self-consistent microscopic calculation quantitatively captures our key observations, establishing an excitonic realization of preformed-pairing physics.

title: Structural Response to the Hidden Charge Order in Sr$_3$Fe$_2$O$_7$
summary: We previously reported `hidden' charge order below $\sim$330 K in the centrosymmetric skyrmion host Sr$_3$Fe$_2$O$_7$ [J.-H. Kim et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 127, 097203 (2021)], finally identifying the charge disproportionation and localization transition that had been first seen in the 1960s. We detected this through resonant x-ray scattering, which directly probes electron density, but is only indirectly sensitive to the lattice structure. This left open the question of whether the charge-ordering transition has a true structural component or consists merely of the reorganization of electrons. Neutrons probe the lattice directly, and we now show, based on neutron data, that the charge order is accompanied by a clear structural modification.

title: Non-Invertible Quantum Cellular Automata I: Microscopic Definition of Non-Invertible Symmetries
summary: We introduce non-invertible quantum cellular automata (QCAs), defined as locality-preserving quantum channels that are dualizable and pure. This provides an operator-algebraic definition of non-invertible symmetries of quantum lattice systems, formulated in terms of their action on local operators. Focusing on quantum spin chains, we motivate these defining conditions and conjecture that every such quantum channel admits a realization by dualizable topological defects or, equivalently, by dualizable sequential quantum circuits. We construct a broad class of examples, including on-site non-invertible symmetries that are anomalous, as well as higher-dimensional examples. In Part II of this work, we reconstruct topological defects whose boundary algebras yield an index theory that classifies non-invertible QCAs up to blend equivalence.

title: Competing Magnetic Orders and Continuously Varying Exponents in $U(1)$ Spin Liquids
summary: Unequal couplings to a common emergent gauge field provide a continuous way to tune competing magnetic instabilities in an effective description of $U(1)$ spin-liquid mixtures. We study this mechanism in quantum electrodynamics in 2+1 dimensions with two families of four-component Dirac fermions. Combining a leading large-$N$ treatment with Schwinger--Dyson equations, we obtain chiral condensates representing N\'eel order in the two sectors. At fixed fermion number, the coupling ratio $\kappa=e_2^2/e_1^2$ controls which condensates develop. Depending on $N$, the phases with a single condensate are connected through either coexistence or a finite interval in which both fermion families remain gapless. The mass-generation thresholds are reciprocal, and the fermion gaps close with Miransky essential singularities. The renormalization group flow has a circular line of fixed points parametrized by the invariant ratio $\kappa$. At the calculated order, gauge-invariant staggered magnetization correlations have continuously varying exponents in the gapless regime, while the exponent for correlations between the two sectors is independent of $\kappa$. These results connect the competition between magnetic orders to a continuous family of critical theories and identify magnetic correlation signatures of the intervening gapless regime.

title: Multiple Field-Induced Transitions, Magnetocaloric Response and Anisotropic Magnetotransport in Orthorhombic RAlGe (R = Dy, Ho)
summary: We present a comprehensive study of the magnetic, thermodynamic, and magnetocaloric properties of single-crystalline DyAlGe and HoAlGe, both members of the RAlGe Weyl semimetal family. Magnetization, heat capacity and transport measurements reveal multiple magnetic phase transitions associated with the evolution of complex magnetic structures. For DyAlGe, the primary magnetic ordering occurs at \textit{$T_{N1}$}= 30.5 K , while HoAlGe orders at a much lower temperature of \textit{$T_{N1}$}= 11.5 K, followed by additional first-order magnetic transitions at 6.6 K and 8 K, respectively. The magnetization isotherms display pronounced anisotropy for the B $\parallel$ a, consistent with competing exchange and crystal-field interactions. The magnetic entropy change ($\Delta S_M$) derived from isothermal magnetization demonstrates a significant magnetocaloric effect (MCE) with sign change in both systems, with a maximum $\Delta S_M$ of $\approx$ 5$-$23 J/kg-K along B $\parallel$ a for a field change of 0$-$7 T. The sign reversal of $\Delta S_M$ across field-induced transitions highlights the complex field-tuned spin configurations. The moderate MCE and magnetic anisotropy suggest that these materials may serve as model systems for studying magnetocaloric effects in topologically nontrivial intermetallics with interplay between localized 4\textit{f} magnetism and crystal symmetry.

title: Hidden convexity of the Eliashberg condensation energy: existence, uniqueness and continuity of the superconducting state
summary: Kiessling, Altshuler and Yuzbashyan conjectured the thermodynamic transition picture for the isotropic Eliashberg spin-chain functional with vanishing Coulomb pseudopotential: the normal state is the unique minimizer above and at a critical temperature, the superconducting minimizer below it is unique up to gauge, and the transition is continuous. We establish the nonlinear part of this picture. In the variables $\rho_n=\sin^2\theta_n$, the condensation energy restricted to the first quadrant is strictly convex, and folding any admissible chain into that quadrant cannot increase its energy. For every positive, non-increasing interaction with power-law decay, hidden convexity and a compactness estimate give existence and uniqueness of the minimizer up to gauge. The normal state minimizes the energy exactly when its quadratic form is non-negative, including marginal stability. Among admissible chains, a positive solution of the nonlinear Eliashberg equations exists exactly when the normal state is linearly unstable and is then unique. For temperature-dependent families with pointwise continuity and locally uniform decay bounds, the minimizing density is continuous in a weighted $\ell^1$ norm. Together with uniqueness of the linear-stability temperature, these results prove the thermodynamic conjectures for the $\gamma$-model, Einstein phonons and general phonon spectra; the phonon applications use separately established spectral input. Finite-dimensional algebraic and convex-analytic components are machine-checked in Lean. The proofs were obtained independently of concurrent work that reaches overlapping conclusions.

title: High-resolution top-down nanopatterning of NbN thin films for superconducting metamaterials
summary: Periodic nanopatterning offers a route to tailoring vortex motion and the electromagnetic response of superconducting films, providing a basis for superconducting metamaterials. Here, we report a high-resolution top-down nanopatterning process for ultrathin epitaxial NbN films on sapphire substrates. Electron-beam lithography using hydrogen silsesquioxane (HSQ) and ZEP 530A resists was optimized through proximity-effect correction and adhesion-layer integration. Dense superconducting nanowire grids with pitches down to 70 nm were fabricated, alongside millimeter-square areas patterned with 100-nm-pitch hole arrays with high pattern fidelity. A thin Si capping layer was found to significantly improve HSQ adhesion on epitaxial NbN. The nanopatterns were successfully transferred into 5-nm-thick NbN films by reactive ion etching (RIE). Structural and dimensional characterization was performed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and atomic force microscopy (AFM), enabling cross-validation of nanoscale feature dimensions and etch quality. Electrical transport measurements reveal periodic resistance minima and switching-current oscillations at magnetic fields set by the hole-array pitch, consistent with enhanced vortex pinning when the vortex configuration matches the patterned lattice. Cryogenic THz time-domain spectroscopy further reveals a reduced superfluid density in the nanopatterned region relative to pristine NbN, while both regions have a spectroscopic superconducting transition near 14 K. These results establish a robust fabrication platform for superconducting nanopatterns targeting vortex pinning, metamaterials, and quantum-device applications.

title: From the Full Fermionic Hilbert Space to the BCS Paired Subspace
summary: Conventional Bardeen--Cooper--Schrieffer (BCS) and number-projected BCS variational treatments are formulated within a paired Hilbert subspace, where modes with opposite momenta and spins are either both empty or both occupied. Here we ask whether this paired subspace can itself be selected energetically from the full fermionic Hilbert space of the attractive reduced BCS model. Using conserved projectors that distinguish singly occupied states from empty and doubly occupied ones, we decompose the full Hilbert space into invariant sectors. A direct energy comparison between sectors shows that, at zero temperature, every ground state at fixed average particle number lies in the paired subspace. The same holds at fixed even particle number, with the comparison preserving the total particle number, while at fixed odd particle number one fermion remains unpaired, as required by parity. Within the resulting paired subspace, minimization over positive generalized-$P$ representations of pseudospin coherent states selects a common phase for the nonzero pair amplitudes and determines their magnitudes. BCS and number-projected BCS states arise as particular minimizers under the respective particle-number constraints.

title: Ab initio Engineering of Topological Superconductivity in Substrate-Supported Magnetic Chains
summary: In this paper, we employ a combination of several first-principles-based approaches to systematically scan chains of several types of magnetic atoms in different chain geometries on top of various overlayers on the Nb(110) surface, to develop a pathway to engineer topological Majorana edge states. Using atomistic spin-model calculations, we first identify a rich variety of magnetic configurations, including ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, spin-spiral, and exotic up-up-down-down states stabilized solely within a second-order Heisenberg model. In the next step, we solve the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations using a band-theoretical method. Depending on the magnetic structure and atomic configuration, the superconducting spectra may exhibit topologically trivial minigaps, broad overlapping Shiba bands, or localized zero-energy edge states accompanied by sizable topological minigaps. In particular, Fe chains on Ag/Nb(110) are found to display pronounced signatures associated with topological superconductivity, including strongly localized zero-energy edge states and indications of Shiba band inversion. We further demonstrate that changes in the spin structure or a small amount of spatial relaxation can substantially modify the superconducting band structure and the localization properties of the edge states.

title: Atomic-scale Imaging of Time Reversal Breaking Supercurrents in $\mathrm{Bi_2Sr_2CaCu_2O_8}$
summary: A persistent mystery of CuO_2-based high temperature superconductivity has been the mechanism and consequences of time reversal ($\mathcal{T}$)-symmetry breaking. Although theoretical hypotheses focus upon persistent electronic currents as a potential cause, these have been invisible to direct experimental probes. That impasse has recently been removed by development of techniques for atomic-scale supercurrent visualization. Here, by imaging the energy-resolved density of electronic states $N(r,E)$ in $\mathrm{Bi_2Sr_2CaCu_2O_8}$, we search for the specific signatures of flowing supercurrents in a disordered $d$-wave superconductor. Employing the strategy of artificial neural networks (ANN) for complex quantum matter visualization, we designed a dual-ANN (VMAP) to efficiently implement $d$-wave supercurrent visualization, achieving imaging of supercurrent speeds $V(r)$ at magnetic fields $|B| \leq \mu T$ in $\mathrm{Bi_2Sr_2CaCu_2O_8}$. Correspondence between specific characteristics of $N(r,E)$ around each supercurrent loop and a quantum "Rosetta Stone" which translates $N(r,E)$ to $V(r)$, emphasizes the validity of $V(r)$ detection and visualization. Then, for hole-densities 0.17 $\leq p \leq$ 0.22 we observe statistically repeatable networks of supercurrent flows. Crucially, these supercurrents satisfy Kirchhoff's law at junctions within each network. Further, theoretical predictions for supercurrent speeds $V$ in disordered $d$-wave superconductors are consistent with measured 1250 m/s $< V <$ 4000 m/s, and with reported magnetic field amplitudes $|B| \approx$ 0.1 mT Thus, detection and visualization of these supercurrent loop networks provides unique perspectives on $\mathcal{T}$-symmetry breaking in cuprates. It also emphasizes the accelerating utility of ANN techniques for physics discovery from high data volume quantum matter research.

title: When Do Tensor Product Paths Matter? A Group-Theoretic Analysis of Equivariant Interatomic Potentials
summary: Tensor-product (TP) layers in equivariant interatomic potentials encode angular interactions through symmetry-allowed paths. Yet local site symmetry can make an allowed path carry no signal after neighbor aggregation. We call this effect Aggregation Cancellation. In a scalar-input first layer, equal-species neighbors on a complete site-symmetry orbit share scalar and radial factors, reducing their angular contribution to a spherical-harmonic orbit sum. If the restricted degree-$l$ representation has no trivial component, this sum and the corresponding path vanish for any learned radial weight. For an ideal $O_h$ octahedral orbit, this removes the $l_\mathrm{edge}=1,2,3$ classes. Beyond the first layer, the factorisation no longer holds, so cancellation is no longer guaranteed; we instead ask whether affected paths remain less important on average. We test the two levels separately in NequIP: matched-radius TiO$_6$ probes examine first-layer cancellation, whereas a within-model CaTiO$_3$ comparison and six OMat24 models examine the importance bias. We then rank paths on training frames, choose the pruning fraction on validation frames, and evaluate frozen masks on held-out tests. At the highest evaluated fraction (60% of 174 paths), force mean absolute error (MAE) changes are 1.42%, 0.04%, and 1.83% for CaTiO$_3$, OMat24 $O_h$-cubic, and OMat24 low-symmetry data, respectively. The masks imply 67.12-71.94% potential TP-operation reduction and 59.77% potential edge multilayer perceptron (MLP) reduction; these are structural proxies, not measured speedups. The results connect local symmetry to path redundancy and pruning robustness in NequIP; transfer to other architectures remains open.

title: Multicomponent Adaptive Sampling Configuration Interaction method in openLOWDIN: positronic and quantum nuclear systems
summary: We present a multicomponent Selective Configuration Interaction (SCI) method based on the deterministic Adaptive Sampling CI (ASCI) algorithm for computing energies and wavefunction properties of molecular systems containing leptons of variable masses, or quantum nuclei. Near-FCI accuracy is achieved by incorporating second-order Epstein-Nesbet perturbation theory or by dressing the Hamiltonian via Davidson's and co-workers shifted-Bk method. We validate the approach through benchmark positronic (e$^+$LiH, e$^+$OH$^-$, e$^+$Mg) and quantum nuclear systems (HCN), establishing a novel protocol for accurate convergence, based on the iterative adaptation of natural orbitals starting from those obtained by considering only cross-particle CISD excitations, to those obtained from SCI variational space, surpassing the accuracy of previous SCI studies. Overall, we show that the present multi-component SCI framework offers a simple, systematically improvable, and cost-effective alternative to traditional CI approaches.

title: Accelerating auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo with mixed-precision random propagators
summary: We develop an algorithm to propagate auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) wavefunctions in mixed precision. We target NVIDIA Tensor Cores using the TensorFloat-32 (TF32) format. We approximate each full-precision array by a TF32 leading term and a TF32 residual, and each full-precision matrix product by three TF32 products accumulated in full precision. Benchmarks on hydrogen chains show that mixed-precision propagation is consistently faster than double-precision GPU propagation, with an increasing advantage as the system size grows. The resulting local-energy deviations remain small over the propagation windows considered here. These results identify the stochastic two-body propagator as a particularly effective target for reduced precision, while our method allows higher precision to be retained for accuracy-sensitive operations. Hence, our algorithm provides a practical way to speed up AFQMC calculations and demonstrates where reduced precision can be applied without adverse effects on the method's accuracy.

title: Efficient strategies for obtaining accurate kinetics from biased simulations
summary: It has been demonstrated that one can recover the unbiased rate constants for slow conformational transitions by observing transitions driven by a bias potential added along one or several collective variables (CVs). However, the choice of CV, biasing scheme, biasing parameters and the rate estimator can all affect the results and it is not obvious which to choose for a given problem. In this study, we compare accuracy versus computational cost for a previously established benchmark system, a coarse-grained protein with computationally accessible unfolding kinetics. We apply bias to four CVs of decreasing quality in both a time-dependent and quasi-static manner, and compare different estimators for the unfolding rate constant in terms of absolute accuracy to the estimated reference unbiased rate. We show that in the case of gentle biasing, the exponential average time-dependent rate (EATR) framework, which simultaneously fits the unbiased rate constant and a coordinate quality metric $\gamma$, recovers accurate kinetics in nearly all cases.For poor CVs, estimators equivalent to assuming a good coordinate ($\gamma=1$) systematically fail regardless of biasing method or parameters. We introduce heuristics to show when we expect the rates to be inaccurate, and identify which combinations of biasing scheme, estimator and number of runs reach a given accuracy at the lowest cost.

title: Neural Network Path Optimization for Finding Transition States on a Machine Learned Potential
summary: Transition states govern chemical reaction rates and outcomes, yet locating them remains a central challenge in computational chemistry. Double-ended search methods find transition states given reactant and product structures, but generally rely on discretized path representations developed for density functional theory, where potential energy surface evaluations are expensive. Machine learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) dramatically reduce this cost and leverage automatic differentiation to access higher-order derivatives efficiently. We introduce Popcornn, a framework to find transition states by optimizing continuous neural network paths atop an MLIP with a parallelized adaptive numerical integrator. This combination eliminates path discretization artifacts, reduces hyperparameter sensitivity, and enables non-local optimization to overcome local features using second-order potential-energy-surface information. Popcornn consistently recovers more correct transition states than standard methods such as nudged elastic band and growing string, across MLIPs on thousands of organic reactions, establishing it as a robust, automation-ready method for high-throughput transition state search. Popcornn's infrastructure is flexible in path objective, integration strategy, and optimization algorithm, making it a practical tool and platform for investigating open questions in MLIP-based path optimization.

title: Spin-free potential-energy curves, spectroscopic constants, and permanent dipole-moment functions for all 18 CO states correlating with the first atomic asymptote
summary: We report ab initio potential-energy curves and permanent dipole-moment functions for all 18 spin-free adiabatic electronic states of $^{12}$C$^{16}$O correlating with the lowest dissociation limit, C($^3$P)+O($^3$P). Our state-averaged CASSCF/icMRCI(+Q) calculations with the aug-cc-pV5Z basis cover the complete set of singlet, triplet, and quintet manifolds. For the ground state, we examine basis-set convergence using the aug-cc-pV$n$Z series ($n=T,Q,5,6$) and extrapolate to the complete-basis-set limit. The resulting potential-energy curves reproduce the established topology of the low-lying CO states, including the double-minimum structure of the 2$^{1}\Sigma^{+}$ state and pronounced adiabatic mixing in several excited states. We determine rovibrational levels and spectroscopic constants for bound states and selected local minima, assess uncertainties, and compare our results with experiment and previous calculations. We find good agreement with experiment for the ground state and well-characterized low-lying singlet and triplet states. For the $1^1\Sigma^+$ ground state, $R_e=1.131~\r{A}$ and $\omega_e=2161.04$~cm$^{-1}$ are both within $0.5\%$ of experiment. The dissociation energy is $D_0=89473\pm141$~cm$^{-1}$. The most strongly bound quintet, $1^5\Pi$, has $D_e=6401$~cm$^{-1}$ and $\omega_e=982~$cm$^{-1}$. The $1^5\Sigma^+$ state has a shallow long-range well with $D_e=849$cm$^{-1}$, while $2^5\Sigma^+$, $2^5\Pi$, and $1^5\Delta$ are predominantly repulsive. Variations in the permanent dipole moments with bond length indicate changes in electronic character and charge redistribution, particularly where adiabatic states interact strongly. These data provide a basis for interpreting rovibrational spectra and for future studies of nonadiabatic effects, spin--orbit coupling, and collision dynamics.

title: Quadrature-Free Radial Intracule Densities: A Bessel-Harmonic Formulation for Gaussian Basis Sets
summary: The radial intracule density $I(R)$, the probability distribution of the interelectronic distance, is a compact and physically transparent picture of electron correlation, but its evaluation for molecules has always relied on a numerical angular quadrature over the orientation of the interelectronic vector. We show that this quadrature can be removed altogether for Cartesian Gaussian basis sets and arbitrary second-order density matrices. Starting from the Hermite Gaussian expansion of the products of basis functions, the coupling exponential $e^{2\mu\mathbf{R}\cdot\mathbf{T}}$ that links radial and angular variables is expanded in modified spherical Bessel functions and real spherical harmonics, and the expansion terminates rigorously at $l=p_x+p_y+p_z$, where the $p$'s are the Cartesian powers arising from the Hermite expansion. The angular average is then exact, the atomic limit reduces to a finite sum of terms $C_iR^{n_i}e^{-\mu R^2}$, and the radial moments $\int_0^\infty R^nI(R)\,dR$ are given in closed form through the confluent hypergeometric function ${}_1F_1$. The scheme is exact in principle and fails only arithmetically: we identify the catastrophic cancellations in the angular-momentum coupling that ruin binary64 evaluations for heavy atoms and remove them by elevating the cancelling chain to binary128. Sum rules for the total, Coulomb and exchange-correlation intracules are recovered to seven to eight significant digits for systems from LiH to Kr$_2$, whereas Euler-Maclaurin and Lebedev quadratures err by up to 22% for stretched or multicenter molecules.

title: Spin-Adapted Neural-Network Backflow Wavefunctions for Excited States of Strongly Correlated Open-Shell Systems
summary: Building on the success of neural-network quantum states (NQS) for molecular ground states, multi-state frameworks such as natural excited states (NES) [Pfau et al., Science 2024, 385, eadn0137] extend NQS to chemically important excited states. However, without control over total spin, such calculations can require the inclusion of many intervening states of other spins, particularly in strongly correlated systems with dense low-energy spectra. We therefore generalize our previously developed spin-adapted neural network backflow (SA-NNBF) ansatz [Li et al., arXiv:2604.06841 (2026)] to improve its variational flexibility for excited-state calculations within a prescribed spin sector. We establish the universality of this extended ansatz within the chosen orbital space and spin sector, and use numerical benchmarks to assess how parameter allocation affects the ansatz's accuracy. With the spin-adapted ansatz, we are able to directly optimize the first excited state (a singlet) of $O_2$ without using any multi-state frameworks. Combining the extended ansatz with NES, we obtain low-lying triplet states of $O_2$ and singlet states of the $[\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{S}_2(\mathrm{SCH}_3)_4]^{2-}$ cluster without including intervening states of other spins. Both the single-state and NES calculations achieve chemical accuracy relative to the exact energies. Our work provides a practical NQS framework for targeting excited states of prescribed spin in strongly correlated systems.

title: Quantum-classical dynamical density functional theory for solvation dynamics
summary: We provide a unified modeling framework for thermalization and non-equilibrium spectroscopy in overdamped polar environments. This framework extends dynamical density functional theory to describe the coupled quantum-classical evolution of a molecular electronic subsystem and an overdamped polar solvent represented by a reaction-field coordinate. The nonadiabatic dynamics is formulated in terms of an operator-valued distribution obeying a quantum-classical Ehrenfest--Smoluchowski equation which exhibits nonlinear classical diffusion and non-increasing free energy, thereby retaining detailed balance. In contrast, a quantum-classical Liouville--Smoluchowski model with quantum-classical linear diffusion develops unstable long-time behavior and fails to reach a stationary thermal state. The method is applied to a two-level model of a polar dye in three different solvents: chloroform, dichloromethane, and dimethyl sulfoxide, each differing in polarity and dielectric relaxation time. Absorption and time-resolved emission spectra are obtained from dipole-dipole correlation functions, capturing the solvent-induced spectral broadening, the dynamic Stokes shift, and the time evolution of the emission bandwidth. The calculated solvent spectral response agrees well with the experimental relaxation trends of the three solvents.

title: Second-Order Polarization Propagator Approximation to the Quadratic Unitary Coupled Cluster Framework I: First-Order Properties
summary: We have developed a new formulation for calculating first-order properties in the quadratic unitary coupled-cluster singles and doubles (qUCCSD) method, using a second-order polarizable propagator approximation. The accuracy and reliability of this new framework of the proposed approach have been assessed through the calculation of ground- and excited-state dipole moments and oscillator strengths for a set of small molecules. The Hermiticity of the UCC similarity-transformed Hamiltonian allows molecular properties to be evaluated without introducing left-hand eigenvectors, thereby simplifying the theoretical formulation and computational procedure. Furthermore, the proposed formulation preserves the size-intensivity of transition moments, a property that is not generally guaranteed within the conventional non-Hermitian equation-of-motion coupled-cluster framework. To assess the performance of the proposed method, we have benchmarked both ground- and excited-state properties for 11 small molecules against the extrapolated full configuration interaction (exFCI) reference values and compared with the conventional coupled cluster singles and doubles (CCSD) and third-order algebraic diagrammatic construction (ADC(3)) results. The qUCCSD method yields average errors comparable to those of CCSD while demonstrating significantly improved accuracy over the ADC(3) method.

title: The MC-QTAIM: Why, How, and When?
summary: The multi-component quantum theory of atoms in molecules (MC-QTAIM) generalizes the original QTAIM framework developed by Richard Bader and colleagues, extending atoms-in-molecules analysis beyond ab initio electronic wavefunctions. MC-QTAIM facilitates the examination of the AIM structure in systems and states that require MC wavefunctions, which describe systems containing multiple distinguishable classes of quantum particles. This advancement broadens the applicability of AIM analysis to a wide range of quantum systems and states that were previously inaccessible. These include exotic molecules, such as positronic species; exotic quantum states, such as superposed proton states in molecules with two- or multi-well potential energy surfaces; and non-adiabatic states of conventional molecules. In this review, I aim to explain the fundamental principles of MC-QTAIM analysis in accessible language and explore some of its potential applications. Additionally, the general formalism for energy partitioning in MC systems, called MC Interacting Quantum Atoms (MC-IQA), is introduced. This scheme unifies the energy partitioning of numerous quantum systems and encompasses the IQA method originally developed by Pendas and colleagues, as well as the previously developed two-component IQA (TC-IQA) scheme - developed by our group to analyze positronic systems - as special cases.

title: A Riemann-invariant contact-capturing scheme with WENO reconstruction and RH-motivated dual-speed dissipation for compressible two-phase mixture flows
summary: This work develops and benchmarks centred (Riemann-solver-free) finite-volume fluxes for a hyperbolic two-phase mixture model with velocity non-equilibrium. The baseline method combines a Riemann-invariant contact-capturing algorithm (RICCA) with dual-speed dissipation and primitive-variable WENO3/WENO5 reconstruction, avoiding full eigen-decomposition while retaining a conservative update. An RH-motivated companion flux (RICCA--RH) is introduced, in which the acoustic weight in $\alpha = |V_n| + Ba$ is controlled by a binary pressure/Rankine--Hugoniot switch. On one-dimensional gas--magma Riemann suite, RICCA--RH tracks legacy RICCA and is sharper than first-order FORCE/Lax--Friedrichs at material contacts; a linearised spectral study clarifies how its dual-speed dissipation differs from FORCE. With WENO5, RICCA, RICCA--RH and FORCE produce essentially identical smooth profiles, indicating that most differences are confined to first-order contact metrics. In two dimensions (gas--liquid benchmarks), the production flux implemented on CPU and Apple Metal reproduces expansion-tube, collision and forward-facing-step patterns and yields intermediate cut-based roughness between RICCA and FORCE. High order is obtained using an approximate face-normal acoustic characteristic reconstruction, a pragmatic multi-variable hybrid sensor, and a Zhang--Shu-style invariant-domain face limiter on $(\rho,\alpha,c)$. An under-dissipative soft-switch variant that rings severely is also documented, and a resident 2D Metal kernel on Apple Silicon is reported to deliver up to $3.9\times$ wall-clock speedup on completed CPU/Metal comparisons (peak on the $101\times101$ expansion tube).

title: Constitutive-fibre mechanics: mechanics-directed uncertainty in constitutive function space
summary: A structural prediction rests on constitutive functions that are known only through a finite number of tests. The tests fix the response along the states they visit; together with a declared regularity bound they leave a set of admissible constitutive functions, which we call the constitutive fibre. Constitutive-fibre mechanics (CFM) computes the range of a quantity of interest over this set. Adjoint solves of the mechanical problem represent the test observations and the quantity of interest as elements of the constitutive function space. The part of the sensitivity of the quantity of interest that is orthogonal to all observation sensitivities is hidden from the tests; for exact data it alone determines the half-width of the prediction, and for data with tolerance the half-width is a finite convex problem in the span of the adjoint representers. Comparing the two values shows whether a new type of test or a more precise test is needed, and a rank-one update ranks candidate tests before they are performed. A learned constitutive class can only under-represent the range; the deficit is computable. Beyond the linear range, an optimality system with state-dependent representers gives the extreme constitutive functions. The same set decides whether the prediction is defined for every admissible constitutive function, which is a different question from its precision. For a phase-field bar with unknown degradation function, 3% of the sensitivity of the stability eigenvalue is hidden and produces 70% of its uncertainty. For an open-hole composite lamina, the coupon that sharpens the compliance most is not the one that makes the prediction valid; validity is proved on a declared cell by a certificate accepted in exact arithmetic.

title: Coordinating integration of multidisciplinary design analysis and optimisation codes with design structure matrices
summary: The integrated analysis and optimisation codes used to design nuclear fusion reactors need to become increasingly large scale, multidisciplinary and complex to computationally verify design requirements more thoroughly and earlier in the design process. Though the manner in which the integrated models are coupled can have significant implications for computational efficiency, the structure of couplings typically remains hidden in the implementation of a design framework. As this problem is not unique to fusion, we frame integrated design problems as applications of the broader field of Multidisciplinary Design Analysis and Optimisation (MDAO). Originally developed for complex system design problems in e.g. aerospace, the MDAO field uses (extended) Design Structure Matrices (DSMs) to display the architecture of integrated analysis and optimisation codes. The aim of this work is to introduce these DSM methods and demonstrate how they can be used to improve the transparency and efficiency of design codes in fusion. As a proof of concept, DSM methods are applied to two case studies: stellarator optimisation with SIMSOPT and the PROCESS systems code. With these cases, we illustrate how a DSM can help identify structural assumptions in the code, and how architectural insight can be used to improve computational efficiency. In particular, we demonstrate the computational impact by modifying the PROCESS solver architecture based on the feedback loops revealed in an automatically generated DSM, yielding a significant reduction in model evaluations. Such architectural changes are considered especially impactful for future design frameworks that combine higher fidelity models with large numbers of inexpensive models.

title: Non-Intrusive Rubin Substructuring for Geometrically Nonlinear Structures via Nonlinear Manifolds
summary: Component mode synthesis enables modular reduction of large structural models, but its extension to geometrically nonlinear systems remains challenging. This work generalizes the Rubin method by introducing a cubic displacement manifold that statically condenses high-frequency free-interface modes onto the retained low-frequency modes and residual attachment modes. The reduced equations of motion, with cubic polynomial restoring forces, are derived by Galerkin projection onto the manifold tangent subspace. The consistency of the reduced forces is guaranteed by the cubic expansion of the component-level reduced manifold. We further present a non-intrusive procedure that combines elastic-force identification with finite-difference estimates of tangent-stiffness derivatives, which allows the reduced model to be constructed from the linear Rubin model and tangent-stiffness evaluations. In the proposed numerical tests, the reduced assembled models accurately reproduce the nonlinear responses of the full finite-element models, including internal resonance and modal coupling. Scalability and significant computational gains are demonstrated with an industrial scale model of a wing-box tip tank assembly, for which an online speed-up of about 24,666 was obtained.

title: OpenPINN/PINO: An Extensible Open-Source Framework for Agent-Assisted Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Neural Operators
summary: Substantial challenges in physics-informed learning have motivated many improvements, but fragmented implementations hinder systematic organization, integration, and comparison. We propose OpenPINN/PINO, an extensible open-source PyTorch framework for physics-informed neural networks and neural operators. Two shared specifications connect problem setup, local computation, and evaluation. Agents support problem formulation, solver planning, and diagnosis. ProblemSpec defines geometry, governing equations, constitutive relations, parameters, initial and boundary conditions, and optional data. MethodSpec configures the model, sampling, loss, optimization, and differentiation. Researchers can register new problem templates and method components, then combine or compare strategies such as Fourier features, residual-adaptive sampling, and self-adaptive loss weighting for a fixed problem. Agents translate natural-language descriptions into specifications, flag missing information, and propose solver plans. The framework validates these specifications and deterministically generates local training and testing code. A diagnostic agent reviews training logs and evaluation results to identify problems and suggest revisions. Three examples show how method choices and agent diagnostics affect accuracy. For viscous Burgers, Fourier features and residual-adaptive sampling each reduced relative $L^2$ error by about $75\%$ from a shared baseline. For periodic Poisson, spectral differentiation reduced mean-free relative $L^2$ error by about $68\%$ across 16 held-out forcings. For a plate with a hole, successive agent diagnoses guided nondimensionalization and optimization. After initial training failure, all three runs met the $10\%$ target, with relative $L^2$ displacement errors of $3.51\%$--$6.31\%$.
